Added to fulvestrant in AKT-pathway-altered tumours, capivasertib improved progression-free survival from 3.1 to 7.3 months: selection also succeeds at the AKT node, but not at mTOR.

Calcineurin inhibitors block calcineurin-NFAT signalling in the pancreatic beta cell, reducing insulin secretion and beta-cell mass and producing new-onset diabetes after transplantation, with tacrolimus carrying the higher risk of the two agents. This mechanism is distinct from the direct beta-cell toxicity and mTORC2-dependent peripheral insulin resistance associated with sirolimus.

Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin A rather than FKBP12; the drug-immunophilin binary complex is the active species. This is the structural reason cyclosporine does not compete with rapamycin for FKBP12 whereas tacrolimus does.
Cyclosporine acts through cyclophilin A rather than FKBP12, but the resulting complex inhibits the same calcineurin phosphatase, giving the shared NFAT-dependent beta-cell toxicity of the class.
The imidazoquinoline scaffold occupies the ATP site of mTOR as well as of PI3K, giving simultaneous blockade of both nodes of the axis.
Dual blockade of class I PI3K was intended to pre-empt the receptor tyrosine kinase-driven AKT rebound that follows mTOR inhibition, but met the same toxicity ceiling.

Prophylactic dexamethasone mouthwash started together with everolimus reduced grade 2 or higher stomatitis far below the incidence reported in earlier everolimus trials without prophylaxis, although the comparison was with historical rates in a single-arm trial. Mucositis nevertheless remains dose-limiting for mTOR-directed agents at higher exposures.
42% of everolimus-treated patients achieved at least 50% angiomyolipoma reduction (EXIST-2).
edges.context: tuberous sclerosis complex and sporadic LAM

edges.mechanism: BOLERO-2 added everolimus to exemestane in HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer progressing on an aromatase inhibitor, improving median PFS from 2.8 to 6.9 months by investigator assessment; overall survival 31.0 versus 26.6 months did not reach significance.
edges.context: HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer after aromatase inhibitor

edges.mechanism: Added to exemestane, everolimus improved median progression-free survival from 2.8 to 6.9 months; the benefit was independent of PIK3CA genotype and overall survival did not reach significance.
edges.context: BOLERO-2, HR-positive HER2-negative, after aromatase inhibitor
edges.notes: Genotype-independence is established; the proposed mechanism, a general brake on translational and metabolic output, remains contested.

edges.mechanism: RADIANT-3 improved PFS from 4.6 to 11.0 months in advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and RADIANT-4 from 3.9 to 11.0 months in non-functional GI and lung NETs; the disease depends on secretory and translational programmes governed by 4E-BP and TOP mRNA control.

Progression-free survival improved from 4.6 to 11.0 months in pancreatic and from 3.9 to 11.0 months in non-functional gastrointestinal and lung neuroendocrine tumours, diseases dependent on 4E-BP and TOP mRNA control.
Approximately 35% of everolimus-treated patients achieved at least 50% SEGA volume reduction versus 0% on placebo (EXIST-1).

Everolimus is approved for TSC-associated SEGA, renal angiomyolipoma and refractory focal seizures on the basis of the EXIST programme; biallelic inactivation of a direct mTORC1 restraint in lesions driven by nothing else is the condition under which a rapalog does what its mechanism predicts.
In TSC, biallelic loss of a direct mTORC1 restraint makes the lesion fully mTORC1-dependent: roughly 35% achieved SEGA volume reduction, 42% angiomyolipoma reduction and 30-40% seizure reduction.
edges.notes: The case in which the rapalog mechanistic rationale is fully borne out, and the standard against which other indications should be judged.

edges.mechanism: PD-1+ CD4 and CD8 T cell fractions fell in the 218-participant everolimus vaccine-response trial, alongside the improvement in haemagglutination-inhibition titre.
edges.context: adults aged 65 or older; 6 weeks before influenza vaccination
edges.notes: Accumulation of PD-1+ exhausted-like cells is one of the defining features of immunosenescence.

edges.mechanism: In the 218-participant vaccine trial, PD-1-positive CD4 and CD8 T cell fractions fell during six weeks of low-dose everolimus, consistent with partial mTORC1 inhibition reversing features of T cell exhaustion in immunosenescence.
edges.context: six weeks before influenza vaccination; adults aged 65 or older
edges.notes: Secondary immunophenotyping endpoint of one randomised trial; unreplicated, and its relation to clinical immune competence is unestablished.

edges.mechanism: Non-infectious pneumonitis occurs in approximately 5-15% of oncology patients; the most serious and least mechanistically understood rapalog toxicity, with the implicated complex unclear.
Non-infectious pneumonitis occurs in roughly 5-15% of oncology patients; the mechanism is incompletely understood and probably immune-mediated, with no clear complex attribution.
edges.notes: The most serious and least mechanistically understood rapalog toxicity; vigilance and discontinuation are the only mitigations.

edges.mechanism: Small uncontrolled series reported variable responses: the 2023 series included one NPRL3 worsening; in 2025 all four NPRL2/NPRL3 participants improved, including two with seizure freedom.
edges.notes: Clinical efficacy and genotype-based response prediction require controlled studies.

edges.mechanism: In renal cell carcinoma progressing after VEGFR-directed therapy, everolimus extended median progression-free survival from 1.9 to 4.9 months in the final analysis of RECORD-1, without an overall survival benefit, consistent with a cytostatic effect on HIF-dependent translation and the angiogenic programme rather than on a cell-autonomous mTORC1 dependency.

Exceptional-responder literature: a durable complete remission in metastatic urothelial carcinoma with a loss-of-function TSC1 mutation alongside an NF2 nonsense mutation, with TSC1 mutations subsequently found in about 8% of 109 further bladder cancers and correlated with everolimus sensitivity; a second complete responder carried two activating MTOR mutations. A prospective basket study selected for proximal-brake lesions was nonetheless negative.
edges.context: case-level responses; prospective biomarker selection not validated
edges.notes: Genotype-directed rapalog therapy outside TSC remains preliminary, and as a basis for routine biomarker selection it is contested.

edges.mechanism: Everolimus lowers mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 and so favours sequestration of eIF4E, but suppression is site-selective: Ser65 and Thr70, which require prior priming and sustained mTORC1 activity, are suppressed, whereas the priming sites Thr37 and Thr46 remain largely phosphorylated. Cap-dependent translation of messages with structured 5' untranslated regions is therefore only partly inhibited.
edges.notes: Indirect activation of the translational repressor through reduced mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation; the drug does not directly activate 4E-BP1.

edges.mechanism: The 40-O-(2-hydroxyethyl) substitution alters pharmacokinetics but not mechanism: everolimus acts only as an FKBP12 binary complex engaging the FRB of mTORC1.
As the FKBP12 complex, everolimus restricts substrate access to assembled mTORC1; S6K1 Thr389 is fully suppressed while 4E-BP1 Thr37/Thr46 is not.

Kinetic rather than absolute selectivity: with prolonged exposure the FKBP12-rapalog complex captures newly synthesised mTOR before its incorporation into mTORC2, so chronic dosing inhibits mTORC2 in many cell types even though preassembled mTORC2 is spared acutely.
edges.context: chronic or prolonged exposure only; preassembled mTORC2 spared acutely
edges.notes: The primary data in [527] are for rapamycin; extension to everolimus is a class-level inference.

edges.mechanism: 42% of patients achieved at least 50% angiomyolipoma volume reduction in EXIST-2, in TSC-associated or sporadic lymphangioleiomyomatosis-associated disease.
edges.context: tuberous sclerosis complex and sporadic LAM; EXIST-2

edges.mechanism: Hyperglycaemia under everolimus has two contributions with different complex attribution: impaired beta-cell insulin secretion, which follows mTORC1 inhibition, and peripheral insulin resistance, which follows the mTORC2 inhibition that develops with prolonged exposure. mTORC2 is the more heavily implicated of the two.
In the 264-participant phase 2a trial, six weeks of BEZ235 plus low-dose everolimus reduced participant-reported infections during one year of follow-up.
edges.notes: This does not isolate the contribution of either drug or establish efficacy in later trials.

edges.mechanism: Allosteric mTORC1 inhibition in lesions with biallelic inactivation of a direct mTORC1 restraint; approximately 35% of patients achieved at least 50% SEGA volume reduction versus 0% on placebo in the EXIST programme.
edges.notes: Covers the composite TSC indication rather than the three distinct EXIST endpoints, which set the standard against which other indications should be judged.

edges.mechanism: Adjunctive everolimus reduced treatment-resistant focal-onset seizures, with 30-40% of patients achieving at least 50% seizure reduction in EXIST-3.
Stomatitis affects roughly 30-60% of patients depending on indication and reflects the mTORC1 dependence of the rapidly renewing oral epithelium; it is dose-limiting in several oncology regimens.
Allosteric mTORC1 inhibition abolishes phosphorylation of the S6K1 hydrophobic motif; S6K1 suppression by rapalogs is complete, in contrast to the partial suppression of 4E-BP1.
KU-0063794 is an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor selective over related PI3K-family kinases, blocking both complexes; used to attribute effects to mTOR rather than to PI3K.
Specific ATP-competitive mTOR inhibition blocks both complexes, including AKT Ser473 phosphorylation by mTORC2.

Metformin activates AMPK indirectly: inhibition of mitochondrial complex I raises AMP and ADP relative to ATP, and at low, clinically relevant concentrations a lysosomal route through PEN2, the v-ATPase, AXIN and LKB1 has been reported by a single laboratory. LKB1 is required for the hepatic effect.
edges.notes: Metformin also inhibits mTORC1 independently of AMPK, through the Rag GTPases and through p53-REDD1.

edges.mechanism: Metformin accumulates in mitochondria and mildly inhibits complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), lowering ATP production and raising AMP/ADP:ATP, the proximal trigger for AMPK activation.
Low-dose metformin binds PEN2, which then engages ATP6AP1 to inhibit v-ATPase, triggering AXIN-LKB1 recruitment to Ragulator and lysosomal AMPK activation without a change in AMP:ATP.
edges.notes: Recent single-group discovery; independent replication limited.

edges.mechanism: Metformin inhibits mTORC1 independently of AMPK and TSC2 in a Rag GTPase-dependent manner; constitutively active Rag mutants blunt the effect, suggesting interference with Rag-mediated lysosomal recruitment.
edges.notes: the Rag step is inferred from constitutively active Rag mutants rather than demonstrated directly.

edges.mechanism: Metformin lowers mTORC1 activity indirectly and does not bind mTOR. One route is AMPK-dependent, through phosphorylation of Raptor at Ser792 and enhancement of TSC2 GAP activity; a second is AMPK-independent, requires the Rag GTPases and was demonstrated in cells lacking AMPK or TSC2. Because of the second route, suppression of mTORC1 cannot be inferred from AMPK activation alone.
edges.notes: The AMPK-independent, Rag-dependent route is dose-dependent and rests on a smaller body of work than the AMPK-dependent route.

edges.mechanism: AMPECT established nab-sirolimus in advanced malignant PEComa, with response enriched in TSC2-mutant tumours.
Albumin-bound sirolimus produced durable responses in advanced malignant PEComa, with response strongly enriched in TSC2-mutant tumours.
The albumin-bound nanoparticle alters delivery and tumour exposure only; the released sirolimus acts through FKBP12 on the FRB of mTORC1 as usual.
Nanoparticle albumin-bound sirolimus delivers sirolimus, which via FKBP12 engages the FRB domain of assembled mTORC1.
OSI-027 binds the mTOR ATP site and suppresses both mTORC1 and mTORC2 signalling, including 4E-BP1 phosphorylation resistant to rapamycin.
edges.notes: ATP-competitive inhibitor of the mTOR kinase domain, documented in the primary literature.

edges.mechanism: Selective ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitor with activity against both mTORC1 and mTORC2.
PP242 occupies the mTOR ATP site and inhibits both complexes; it defined the rapamycin-resistant outputs of mTORC1 alongside Torin1.
Active-site inhibition blocks rapamycin-resistant outputs of mTORC1 and also inhibits mTORC2, abolishing AKT Ser473 phosphorylation.
The tethered ATP-site moiety delivers complete catalytic inhibition once the molecule is anchored through FKBP12, so inhibition does not depend on the allosteric effect alone.
The rapamycin end of the bi-steric molecule recruits FKBP12; the resulting avidity for the FRB-bearing complex is what confers mTORC1 selectivity on an otherwise non-selective ATP-site warhead.
FKBP12-RapaLink-1 engages the FRB domain, providing the anchoring half of the bi-steric mechanism.
Bivalent engagement of FRB and the ATP cleft on the same mTOR protomer gives an avidity-driven potency far above either moiety alone.
Bivalent engagement gives complete mTORC1 suppression and retains activity against FRB resistance mutations that abolish rapalog binding, establishing the bi-steric concept.

RapaLink-1 crosses the blood-brain barrier and accumulates in intracranial tumour tissue to a degree the first- and second-generation agents do not, which is the basis of its preclinical activity in glioblastoma models.
edges.context: preclinical glioblastoma models; no human data
edges.notes: Bears on the pharmacokinetic constraint that restricted CNS access limits every neurological indication.

edges.mechanism: RapaLink-1 tethers rapamycin to an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor, so that FKBP12-rapamycin anchoring at the FRB domain delivers the active-site moiety with high avidity. Potency is therefore retained against FRB-domain substitutions such as A2034V and F2108L, which weaken FKBP12-rapamycin binding and confer rapalog resistance, and against the kinase-domain substitution M2327I, which confers resistance to ATP-competitive inhibitors used alone.
edges.context: FRB-domain and kinase-domain mTOR resistance mutants

edges.mechanism: Rapamycin has no direct activity on mTOR; it first binds the immunophilin FKBP12 and the binary complex is the active species. The yeast FPR1 screen established this genetically.
Rapamycin binds the FKBP12 immunophilin with low-nanomolar affinity; the binary complex, not free drug, is the inhibitory species, so FKBP12 is obligatory for all rapalog action.
Rapamycin is the drug half of the composite inhibitor; neither partner alone binds FRB with meaningful affinity.
Rapamycin contributes the second half of the composite surface, its effector domain projecting away from FKBP12 to contact the FRB domain of mTOR.

Rapalogs suppress cap-dependent translation only partially. With FKBP12-rapamycin bound to the FRB domain, phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 at Ser65 and Thr70 is blocked while Thr37 and Thr46 remain largely phosphorylated, so eIF4F assembly continues at a substantial rate. The limitation is structural rather than a matter of dose.
edges.notes: ATP-competitive and bi-steric inhibitors suppress cap-dependent translation far more completely.

edges.mechanism: Rapamycin blocks phosphorylation of the late 4E-BP1 sites Ser65 and Thr70 while largely sparing the priming sites Thr37 and Thr46, so binding of 4E-BP1 to eIF4E is only partly restored and cap-dependent translation continues. The limitation is structural rather than a matter of dose.
edges.notes: The degree of resistance varies with cell type, and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation can recover during prolonged exposure.

edges.mechanism: Thr37/Thr46 phosphorylation is relatively rapamycin-resistant in many experimental settings, limiting restoration of 4E-BP1-mediated repression of eIF4E.
edges.notes: Phosphosite sensitivity and the resulting translational response depend on cell type and exposure.

edges.mechanism: Rapamycin lowers activating Ser44 phosphorylation of TIF-IA/RRN3 and raises the inhibitory Ser199 site, blocks the S6K1-dependent phosphorylation of the UBF carboxy-terminal activation domain, and relieves mTORC1 repression of MAF1 — collapsing Pol I 47S pre-rRNA synthesis and Pol III tRNA/5S output together.
edges.notes: Rapamycin acts on both polymerase arms: phosphorylation of TIF-IA and of the UBF carboxy-terminal activation domain falls rapidly, while MAF1 escapes mTORC1-dependent inactivation and continues to repress RNA polymerase III.

edges.mechanism: FKBP12-rapamycin bound to the mTORC1 FRB domain abolishes S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation completely, in contrast to its partial effect on 4E-BP1. This makes Thr389 the pharmacodynamic marker of mTORC1 engagement and the readout against which partial pathway inhibition is judged in dosing studies.
Prolonged rapamycin exposure inhibits mTORC2 because FKBP12–rapamycin captures newly synthesised mTOR before assembly; mTORC1 selectivity is kinetic, not absolute.
Chronic dosing lowers mTORC2 output, including AKT Ser473, in many but not all cell types, by blocking assembly of new complexes; selectivity for mTORC1 is therefore kinetic rather than absolute.
edges.notes: Cell-type variability in mTORC2 sensitivity is itself well replicated.

edges.mechanism: Chronic rapamycin exposure disrupts mTORC2 and causes insulin resistance, an effect uncoupled from its longevity benefit.
edges.notes: Whether intermittent dosing, which allows mTORC2 to recover between doses, spares glucose metabolism remains unsettled; the supporting evidence is preliminary [12].

edges.mechanism: Intermittent dosing allows mTORC2 to recover between doses; preclinical data and low-exposure human cohorts without dysglycaemia support this but no powered trial has tested it.
edges.notes: Evidence is emerging rather than established.

edges.mechanism: Pharmacological mTOR inhibition lengthens circadian period and alters amplitude in central and peripheral clocks, so mTOR activity sets clock pace as well as responding to it.
Low-dose rapamycin improved circadian reporter amplitude in engineered U2OS cells expressing SKS-associated MTOR variants.
edges.context: engineered U2OS reporter cells; not patient-derived cells

edges.mechanism: Low-dose rapamycin improved circadian reporter amplitude in engineered U2OS cells expressing SKS-associated MTOR variants.
edges.context: engineered U2OS reporter cells; not patient-derived cells

edges.mechanism: Rapamycin lengthens the free-running circadian period, the specific readout behind the general statement that mTOR inhibition modulates central and peripheral clock function
High-dose rapamycin precipitated delayed sleep–wake phase disorder in some Smith–Kingsmore patients, whereas low doses improved sleep: dose and timing interact with sleep architecture.
edges.notes: That mTOR-directed therapy has a chronobiology is well established, but the optimal dosing time for any indication remains unresolved.

edges.mechanism: Higher-dose rapamycin precipitated delayed sleep-wake phase disorder in some Smith-Kingsmore patients, the mirror image of the low-dose benefit on circadian amplitude.
edges.notes: Clearest human evidence that mTOR-directed therapy in the nervous system is dose- and time-dependent in direction.

edges.mechanism: Rapamycin substantially extends the lifespan of Bmal1-null mice, the key in vivo evidence that their shortened lifespan is mTORC1-dependent.

Encapsulated rapamycin begun at 600 days of age extended median and maximal lifespan of genetically heterogeneous mice at three independent sites, raising the age at 90% mortality by 9% in males and 14% in females; a threefold higher dose of 42 ppm increased median lifespan by 23% in males and 26% in females, and treatment begun at 20 months extends survival even when given for only three months or in alternating months.
edges.notes: Continuous exposure is not required for lifespan extension, although the benefit of brief or intermittent dosing is sex-dependent.

edges.mechanism: Encapsulated rapamycin begun at 600 days of age raised age at 90% mortality by 9% in male and 14% in female genetically heterogeneous mice at three independent sites; a threefold higher dietary dose of 42 ppm raised median lifespan by 23% in males and 26% in females, and late-life intermittent regimens also extended survival.
edges.context: genetically heterogeneous mice, Interventions Testing Program
edges.notes: Genetic reduction of mTOR or S6K1 reproduces the effect, supporting on-target action; translation beyond rodents is unproven.

edges.mechanism: Pharmacological mTORC1 inhibition reverses the consequences of unrestrained mTORC1 in Bmal1-null animals, delaying their premature-ageing phenotypes and substantially extending lifespan
Uncontrolled SKS observations linked rapamycin exposure to altered sleep; improvement after dose reduction included concomitant suvorexant in the detailed case.
edges.notes: The contribution of rapamycin could not be isolated from concomitant treatment.

edges.mechanism: Rapamycin reduces brain amyloid-beta and improves cognition in 3xTg-AD mice, with benefit dependent on intact autophagy and on early initiation.
edges.notes: Largely confined to treatment begun before substantial pathology accumulates.

edges.mechanism: Pharmacological mTOR inhibition induces autophagy and accelerates clearance of misfolded aggregates in cellular and animal models; this is the whole basis of the neurodegeneration rationale.
Relieving mTORC1 repression of ULK1 and TFEB induces autophagy and accelerates clearance of amyloid-beta, alpha-synuclein and polyglutamine aggregates in cellular and animal models.
edges.notes: No controlled human efficacy data exist in neurodegenerative disease.

edges.mechanism: Rapamycin reduces brain amyloid-beta and improves cognition in 3xTg-AD mice, with benefit dependent on intact autophagy and largely confined to treatment initiated before substantial pathology accumulates.
edges.context: 3xTg-AD mice; ERAP phase IIa under way in humans
edges.notes: No controlled human efficacy data exist.

edges.mechanism: Sirolimus-class agents have real but largely cytostatic antitumour activity: albumin-bound sirolimus is approved for advanced malignant perivascular epithelioid cell tumour, with response enriched in TSC2-mutant tumours, while no randomised trial of a rapalog in a solid tumour has shown a significant overall survival benefit. Separately, deferral of lethal neoplasia may account for part of the lifespan extension rapamycin produces in mice.
edges.context: advanced solid tumours; mouse lifespan studies
edges.notes: What is disputed is the mechanism of murine lifespan extension, not the existence of antitumour activity.

edges.mechanism: Rapamycin or CCI-779 reduces aggregates and improves outcomes in fly and mouse models of Huntington's disease.
In kidney transplant recipients without pre-existing diabetes sirolimus was independently associated with new-onset diabetes, adjusted hazard ratios roughly 1.4-1.7.
edges.notes: Combines direct beta-cell toxicity with peripheral insulin resistance from chronic mTORC2 loss.

edges.mechanism: In kidney transplant recipients without pre-existing diabetes, sirolimus was independently associated with new-onset diabetes across regimens, with adjusted hazard ratios of roughly 1.4-1.7.
edges.notes: The diabetogenic signal is clearest at high continuous exposures; extrapolation to intermittent low-dose use is not supported.

edges.mechanism: Rapamycin protects dopaminergic neurons in cellular and rodent models of Parkinson disease; in those models protection tracked with blocked production of the stress protein RTP801/REDD1 and preserved AKT phosphorylation, whereas the catalytic inhibitor Torin1 was not protective. Enhanced autophagic clearance of alpha-synuclein is a separate route shown in other model systems.
Rapamycin prevents seizures after depletion of STRADA in models of PMSE, with support from preclinical work and small clinical series.
mTOR inhibition with rapamycin or CCI-779 induces autophagy and reduces polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin aggregates and toxicity in fly and mouse models.

Direct beta-cell toxicity of rapamycin: reduced insulin secretion, disturbed calcium handling and mitochondrial dysfunction; one of the two components of NODAT alongside mTORC2-dependent peripheral insulin resistance.
Rapamycin blocks L-LTP while sparing the early phase, which is the pharmacological demonstration that the late phase is protein-synthesis dependent.

mTORC1 drives the adaptive growth of cardiomyocytes, so partial inhibition blunts physiological hypertrophy; the same inhibition attenuates pathological hypertrophy in multiple models and regresses established pressure-overload hypertrophy, so the adaptive and maladaptive arms are not separable pharmacologically.
Low-dose rapamycin during acute viral infection enhances the quantity and functional quality of memory CD8 T cells, T cell-intrinsically and across infection models.
edges.context: low dose, acute viral infection; reproduced in non-human primates
edges.notes: The CD8 memory paradox: partial inhibition improves rather than suppresses one arm of adaptive immunity.

edges.mechanism: Low-dose rapamycin given during acute viral infection increases both the quantity and the functional quality of memory CD8 T cells, T cell-intrinsically and across infection models and in primates.
Cytopenias follow from the proliferative requirement for mTORC1 in haematopoiesis.
Haematopoietic progenitors require mTORC1 for proliferation, so suppression produces anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia; dose reduction is the standard response.
Hyperglycaemia at immunosuppressive exposures reflects hepatic, adipose and beta-cell physiology, chiefly through loss of mTORC2 signalling.
edges.notes: Contrast RMC-5552, where hyperglycaemia occurred in only 4% despite complete mTORC1 blockade.

edges.mechanism: Chronic exposure raises glucose through combined beta-cell dysfunction and mTORC2-dependent peripheral insulin resistance; attribution is mTORC2 greater than mTORC1.
edges.notes: Whether intermittent low-exposure regimens avoid this effect is unresolved.

edges.mechanism: Rapamycin partially corrects the hyperphagic obesity of POMC-neuron Tsc1 deletion.

Hypothalamic mTORC1 acts as a nutrient sensor in the arcuate nucleus: rapamycin abolishes the anorectic response to intracerebroventricular leucine and partially corrects the hyperphagic obesity produced by Tsc1 deletion in POMC neurons. This raises the possibility that part of the metabolic toxicity attributed to liver, adipose and beta cell is centrally mediated.
edges.notes: This makes tissue-level attribution of metabolic toxicity from peripheral measurements less secure than it appears.

edges.mechanism: Hypertriglyceridaemia and hypercholesterolaemia on mTOR inhibitors reflect altered hepatic and adipose lipid handling, with both complexes implicated.
edges.notes: Dyslipidaemia is the adipose and hepatic consequence of mTOR inhibition.

edges.mechanism: Altered hepatic and adipose lipid handling under inhibition of both complexes raises triglycerides and cholesterol in a dose-related manner; monitoring and statin therapy are the usual mitigation.
In PEARL, lean tissue mass increased rather than decreased in women on 10 mg weekly compounded rapamycin; a secondary, sex-restricted finding at very low exposure.
edges.notes: Subgroup analysis; no trough concentrations measured. Reassuring but not evidence of efficacy.

edges.mechanism: In the PEARL trial, lean tissue mass increased rather than decreased in women receiving 10 mg weekly compounded rapamycin, against the anabolic-resistance concern that chronic mTORC1 inhibition should reduce muscle mass in older adults.
edges.context: women, 10 mg weekly compounded sirolimus, 48 weeks; secondary endpoint, exposure not confirmed by trough measurement
edges.notes: Lean-mass monitoring is one of the measurements a serious geroscience trial must include; the direction of effect is unresolved, hence 'modulates'.

edges.mechanism: urinalysis monitoring is the stated mitigation.
Podocytes require mTORC1 for maintenance and autophagic flux, so inhibition can produce proteinuria; urinalysis monitoring is the recommended surveillance.

Chronic mTORC1 inhibition is predicted to impair the anabolic response of skeletal muscle and to promote sarcopenia; acute rapamycin blocks the contraction-induced rise in human muscle protein synthesis, whereas intermittent low-dose exposure has not produced measurable muscle loss and was associated with increased lean tissue mass in one randomised trial. Whether intermittent dosing preserves the acute anabolic response while lowering chronic tone is unresolved.
edges.notes: Human data conflict across exposures, and no trial has tested chronic dosing against a muscle-mass endpoint in older adults.

edges.mechanism: Rapalog stomatitis follows from mTORC1 dependence of renewing oral epithelium and is substantially preventable with topical dexamethasone or tacrolimus prophylaxis.
edges.notes: The only self-reported adverse event significantly more frequent among off-label users.

edges.mechanism: Loss of mTORC1-dependent renewal in oral epithelium produces aphthous-type ulceration in roughly 30-60% of patients, the commonest dose-limiting rapalog toxicity in oncology.
Rapamycin expands regulatory T cells preferentially, which is the basis of its immunosuppressive use.
mTOR inhibition blocks Th1, Th2 and Th17 differentiation while permitting Foxp3+ regulatory T cell differentiation and expansion, which underlies the immunosuppressive use of the drug.
Rapamycin suppresses the SASP without eliminating senescent cells, so a drug can give geroprotective benefit by attenuating consequences of a process it did not cause.
edges.notes: Suppression of the SASP by rapamycin shows that an intervention is effective, which does not by itself establish causal primacy.

edges.mechanism: Alpha-synuclein is degraded by both macroautophagy and the proteasome, and mTOR inhibition with rapamycin induces autophagy and lowers alpha-synuclein levels in cell models; rapamycin also protects dopaminergic neurons in rodent models of Parkinson disease.
edges.context: cellular and rodent models of Parkinson disease

edges.mechanism: Two opposing effects: relief of S6K1-IRS-1 feedback raises PI3K-dependent Thr308 signalling, while prolonged mTORC2 depletion lowers Ser473. Net direction depends on exposure duration and cell type.
Suppression of mTORC1-dependent effector lymphocyte expansion prevents renal allograft rejection; this was the first approved indication and is given at continuous, trough-monitored exposures.

Sirolimus stabilises lung function in lymphangioleiomyomatosis, whose lesional cells carry biallelic TSC2 inactivation with constitutive mTORC1 activation as the principal driver; it also reduces serum VEGF-D and improves symptoms.
mTORC1 phosphorylation stabilises Grb10, an inhibitor of insulin and IGF-1 receptor signalling; drug-induced loss of that stabilisation removes a second brake on upstream flux.
Inhibiting mTORC1 removes S6K1-mediated inhibitory serine phosphorylation of IRS-1, stabilising it and restoring insulin- and IGF-1-driven PI3K output: the feedback arm of AKT rebound.
Acute inhibition is complex-selective because only mTORC1 presents an accessible FRB; suppression is substrate-selective, complete for S6K1 and incomplete for 4E-BP1.

Rapamycin reduces brain amyloid-beta and improves cognition in 3xTg-AD mice, with benefit dependent on intact autophagy and largely confined to treatment initiated before substantial pathology accumulates.
edges.context: 3xTg-AD mice; benefit requires intact autophagy and early initiation; no controlled human efficacy data
edges.notes: No controlled human efficacy data exist.

edges.mechanism: Inhibition of mTOR raises plasma cholesterol alongside triglycerides through reduced lipoprotein lipase activity, increased adipose lipolysis and impaired clearance of apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins; the effect is dose-related at therapeutic exposures and is managed by lipid monitoring and statin therapy.
edges.notes: Hypercholesterolaemia and hypertriglyceridaemia arise from the same disturbance of hepatic and adipose lipid handling and usually occur together.

edges.mechanism: Suppressed angiogenesis and fibroblast proliferation delay surgical healing, which is why planned perioperative interruption is advised before elective surgery.
Suppression of effector lymphocyte expansion raises infection risk at immunosuppressive exposures; dose, schedule and vaccination timing are the available levers.
edges.notes: Contrasts with enhanced vaccine and CD8 memory responses at low, partial-inhibition exposures.

edges.mechanism: Prolonged dosing disrupts mTORC2 in liver, muscle and adipose tissue, producing insulin resistance that is mechanistically separable from the longevity benefit in mice.

Rapamycin blocks hypertrophy in response to IGF-1, mechanical overload and chronic stimulation, and blocks the contraction-induced rise in human muscle protein synthesis, showing that mTORC1 activity is required for load-induced muscle growth.
edges.context: rodent overload models and human contraction studies
edges.notes: Ageing muscle already responds less strongly to loading and to amino acids, so lean mass is the principal concern during chronic exposure in older adults.

edges.mechanism: Non-infectious pneumonitis occurs in roughly 5-15% of oncology patients treated with rapalogs and is the most serious and least well understood toxicity of the class. It is probably immune-mediated rather than a direct consequence of mTORC1 blockade in lung epithelium, and management rests on vigilance, dose interruption and discontinuation.
edges.notes: Reported for both sirolimus and everolimus; the best-characterised series come from everolimus-treated renal cell carcinoma.

edges.mechanism: Induction of macroautophagy accelerates clearance of alpha-synuclein and polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin, reducing aggregate burden and improving outcomes in fly and mouse models.
Acute rapamycin blocks the contraction-induced rise in human muscle protein synthesis, and mTORC1 activation is required for the response to essential amino acids.
edges.notes: The tissue most clearly requiring mTORC1 is also the one most at risk from chronic inhibition in older adults.

edges.mechanism: Ridaforolimus binds FKBP12, and the binary complex engages the exposed FRB domain of assembled mTORC1, inhibiting the kinase allosterically as for the other first-generation rapalogs.
FKBP12-ridaforolimus complex binds the exposed FRB domain of assembled mTORC1 and sterically restricts substrate access.

RMC-5552 tethers an FKBP12-rapamycin moiety to an ATP-site moiety; FKBP12-mediated avidity confers mTORC1 selectivity while the ATP-site moiety blocks catalysis. Phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 at all four sites, including the rapamycin-resistant priming sites Thr37 and Thr46, is therefore suppressed, and hypophosphorylated 4E-BP1 binds eIF4E. The activation of the repressor is indirect, through inhibition of mTORC1 kinase activity.
edges.notes: Whether complete suppression of 4E-BP1 phosphorylation translates into genotype-dependent clinical benefit is not yet established.

edges.mechanism: The bi-steric design tethers an FKBP12-rapamycin moiety to an ATP-site moiety; FKBP12-mediated avidity confers mTORC1 selectivity while the ATP-site moiety delivers complete catalytic inhibition, so both S6K1 Thr389 and 4E-BP1 are fully suppressed while mTORC2 is relatively spared.
edges.notes: RMC-5552 suppresses both S6K1 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation fully while relatively sparing mTORC2. The effect on S6K1 is indirect, through inhibition of mTORC1 kinase activity.

edges.mechanism: Complete response ongoing beyond six months, with clearance of pathway variants from circulating tumour DNA, in a patient with PTEN- and PIK3CA-altered endometrial cancer; 58% of enrolled patients carried pathogenic mTOR-pathway variants.
edges.notes: A single response is an observation rather than a result.

edges.mechanism: One patient with PTEN- and PIK3CA-altered endometrial cancer achieved a complete response ongoing beyond six months, with clearance of pathway variants from circulating tumour DNA.
edges.context: single case within a phase 1 dose-escalation study
edges.notes: A single response is an observation rather than a result; the evidence remains preliminary.

edges.mechanism: The ATP-competitive moiety occupies the kinase cleft, delivering complete catalytic inhibition of the FRB-anchored complex and thereby full suppression of both S6K1 and 4E-BP1 while mTORC2 is relatively spared.
edges.notes: Explains the dissociation of complete mTORC1 pathway blockade from metabolic toxicity (hyperglycaemia 4%).

edges.mechanism: In 57 patients with advanced solid tumours, disease control was reached in 64% at active doses and one PTEN- and PIK3CA-altered endometrial cancer achieved a complete response with clearance of variants from ctDNA.
edges.context: first-in-human phase 1, 58% with pathogenic mTOR-pathway variants
edges.notes: A single-arm disease-control rate is not an efficacy endpoint; the genotype-dependence prediction remains preliminary.

edges.mechanism: The bi-steric agent carries an FKBP12-rapamycin moiety tethered by a linker to an ATP-site moiety; FKBP12 binding supplies the avidity that confers mTORC1 selectivity.
The FKBP12-bound moiety engages the exposed FRB domain of assembled mTORC1, anchoring the molecule and delivering the tethered ATP-site moiety to the kinase cleft of the same protomer.
RMC-5552 was designed for mTORC1 selectivity with complete pathway suppression, exploiting FKBP12-mediated avidity for the complex whose FRB is exposed.
mTORC2 is relatively spared because engagement depends on an accessible FRB; the clinical correlate is treatment-related hyperglycaemia in only 4% despite complete mTORC1 blockade.
edges.notes: Sparing is relative, not absolute, and rests on a single-arm phase 1 dataset.

edges.mechanism: Treatment-related fatigue in 42% of patients in the first-in-human dose-escalation study.
edges.notes: The frequency comes from one uncontrolled dose-escalation cohort and has not been independently replicated.

edges.mechanism: Treatment-related hyperglycaemia occurred in only 4% and was not dose-limiting despite complete mTORC1 pathway suppression: the dissociation of efficacy from metabolic toxicity predicted by mTORC2 sparing.
edges.notes: The most direct available human evidence, but from a single uncontrolled study.

edges.mechanism: Second most frequent treatment-related adverse event (44%) in the 57-patient first-in-human dose-escalation study.
edges.context: phase 1 dose escalation, intravenous weekly dosing
edges.notes: The frequency comes from one uncontrolled dose-escalation cohort and has not been independently replicated.

edges.mechanism: Mucositis occurred in 49% of 57 patients and grade 3 mucositis was dose-limiting at 10 mg or above, making it the characteristic limitation of the bi-steric generation.
edges.notes: Single-arm dose-escalation data; the direction is consistent with the oral-epithelial toxicity seen with allosteric rapalogs.

edges.mechanism: Expression of interferon-stimulated antiviral genes rose in older adults given RTB101 with low-dose everolimus for six weeks in a 264-participant phase 2a trial, the arm in which infection rates over the following year were also lower.
edges.context: phase 2a; 264 older adults; six weeks of dosing
edges.notes: Antiviral transcript changes are a biomarker, not proof of clinical benefit.

edges.mechanism: RTB101 (BEZ235/dactolisib) is an ATP-competitive PI3K/mTOR inhibitor. At the low exposures studied in older adults, the intended pharmacodynamic effect was preferential TORC1 inhibition.
edges.notes: The immune-function trials did not establish a lifespan benefit.

edges.mechanism: In the 264-participant phase 2a trial, six weeks of RTB101 with low-dose everolimus reduced participant-reported infections during one year of follow-up.
edges.notes: This does not isolate the contribution of either drug or establish efficacy in later trials.

edges.mechanism: The 1024-participant phase 3 trial did not meet its clinically symptomatic respiratory-illness endpoint. Phase 2b had found a signal for laboratory-confirmed infections with RTB101 monotherapy, while its combination comparison was not significant.
edges.notes: Different endpoints and study populations limit cross-trial comparisons; failure cannot be attributed to removal of everolimus.

edges.mechanism: BEZ235 inhibits class I PI3K at sufficient concentrations; this biochemical target profile does not demonstrate substantial PI3K inhibition at the low doses used in the ageing trials.
edges.notes: Target inhibition depends on exposure; the clinical studies described RTB101 as a TORC1 inhibitor.

edges.mechanism: ATP-competitive mTOR inhibition regulates AKT biphasically. Catalytic blockade of mTORC2 abolishes Ser473 phosphorylation and suppresses AKT activity acutely; relief of S6K1-IRS-1 and Grb10 feedback then drives receptor tyrosine kinase-dependent PI3K signalling, so Thr308 phosphorylation and AKT activity rebound while Ser473 phosphorylation remains suppressed.
edges.context: class effect of ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors
edges.notes: The rebound is a principal reason why superior pathway suppression did not translate into clinical efficacy for this class.

edges.mechanism: ATP-competitive occupancy of the mTOR kinase cleft suppresses phosphorylation of all four principal 4E-BP1 sites, including Thr37 and Thr46, which allosteric rapalogs leave largely intact. Hypophosphorylated 4E-BP1 is the active form, so eIF4E is sequestered and cap-dependent translation of mRNAs with structured 5' untranslated regions is blocked.
edges.notes: Indirect activation of the translational repressor through reduced mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation; the drug does not directly activate 4E-BP1.

edges.mechanism: Occupying the ATP cleft blocks catalysis outright, suppressing all mTORC1 outputs including the rapamycin-resistant 4E-BP1 Thr37/Thr46 sites.
Because the kinase cleft is identical in both complexes and is not occluded by Rictor or mSin1, ATP-competitive agents abolish mTORC2 output including AKT Ser473.
Complete inhibition of both complexes adds mTORC2-dependent hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance to the rapalog toxicity profile, which is the toxicity ceiling that limited this generation.
edges.notes: Attribution of the glycaemic component to mTORC2 rests chiefly on reference [325].

edges.mechanism: Catalytic inhibition of mTORC2 removes AKT Ser473 phosphorylation in liver, adipose tissue and skeletal muscle. Reduced AKT output releases FOXO1-driven hepatic gluconeogenesis and impairs insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, so insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia are added to the metabolic profile of the allosteric agents.

ATP-competitive inhibition of the mTOR catalytic site abolishes phosphorylation of S6K1 at the Thr389 hydrophobic motif completely, in contrast with the partial and substrate-selective suppression achieved by allosteric agents.

Calcineurin inhibition in the pancreatic beta cell impairs insulin secretion and promotes beta-cell apoptosis, which is the principal mechanism of new-onset diabetes after transplantation in tacrolimus-based regimens.
edges.notes: Sirolimus independently raises the risk of post-transplant diabetes, so the two immunosuppressant classes contribute separately.

edges.mechanism: FK506 binds the same immunophilin as rapamycin but presents a different effector surface, so the FKBP12-FK506 complex engages calcineurin rather than the FRB of mTOR.
FK506 and rapamycin compete for the same FKBP12 binding pocket, so co-exposure antagonises formation of the mTORC1-inhibitory complex: a pharmacodynamic interaction relevant to combined regimens.
Topical tacrolimus mouthwash prophylaxis reduced mucositis from 65% to 31% in the 8-12 mg cohorts of the RMC-5552 phase 1 study; systemic exposure is not the object.
edges.notes: Single-arm comparison within a dose-escalation study.

edges.mechanism: The FKBP12-FK506 complex binds and inhibits the calcineurin phosphatase, blocking NFAT dephosphorylation and IL-2 transcription; this is a distinct mechanism from mTOR inhibition.
Temsirolimus improved overall survival versus interferon-alpha in the Global ARCC trial in poor-prognosis advanced renal cell carcinoma.
edges.notes: Basis of the approved indication in poor-prognosis advanced renal cell carcinoma.

edges.mechanism: Temsirolimus binds FKBP12, and the binary complex engages the exposed FRB domain of assembled mTORC1 by the same allosteric mechanism as the parent macrolide.

Temsirolimus binds FKBP12 and the binary complex engages the exposed FRB domain of assembled mTORC1, sterically restricting substrate access; it is given intravenously as an ester prodrug converted to sirolimus, which contributes much of the effect in vivo.
CCI-779 (temsirolimus), the soluble ester analogue of rapamycin, induces autophagy and reduces polyglutamine aggregate burden and toxicity in fly and mouse models of Huntington disease.
edges.context: fly and mouse Huntington disease models

edges.mechanism: Temsirolimus is given intravenously as an ester prodrug and is hydrolysed to sirolimus, which accounts for much of its systemic exposure and activity.

ATP-competitive occupancy of the mTOR kinase cleft suppresses the rapamycin-resistant 4E-BP1 Thr37/Thr46 sites, so 4E-BP1 remains eIF4E-bound, eIF4F does not assemble, and cap-dependent initiation is blocked far more completely than with rapamycin.

By occupying the ATP site of mTOR, Torin1 blocks phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 at all four sites, including the priming sites Thr37 and Thr46 that resist rapamycin, and cellular phosphatases then remove the existing phosphates. Hypophosphorylated 4E-BP1 sequesters eIF4E, so the activation of the repressor is indirect, through inhibition of the mTOR kinase.
edges.notes: Complete suppression of 4E-BP1 phosphorylation requires catalytic-site rather than allosteric inhibition. Other ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors act the same way, among them PP242, KU-0063794 and AZD8055; sapanisertib and vistusertib belong to the same class.

edges.mechanism: ATP-competitive mTOR inhibition abolishes S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation together with the rapamycin-resistant outputs of mTORC1, so mTORC1 signalling is suppressed completely rather than partially. The effect on S6K1 is indirect, through inhibition of the mTOR kinase.
Torin1 inhibits mTORC1 catalysis directly at the ATP site and was the tool compound that revealed rapamycin-resistant mTORC1 functions.
Torin1 blocks mTORC2 as well, abolishing AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, and is used experimentally to separate complex-selective from pan-mTOR effects.

Torin2 occupies the mTOR ATP-binding cleft and inhibits both complexes, including the rapamycin-resistant 4E-BP1 sites. It is more potent and more orally bioavailable than Torin1 but also inhibits the related PIKK family members ATM, ATR and DNA-PK, so selectivity for mTOR is incomplete at higher concentrations.
edges.notes: Used as a laboratory tool compound rather than a clinical agent.

edges.mechanism: Substitution of the critical serine contact in the FRB domain of human mTOR, Ser2035, abolishes docking of the FKBP12-rapamycin complex while leaving kinase activity intact. FRB substitutions selected under prolonged rapamycin exposure, Ala2034Val and Phe2108Leu, confer rapalog resistance by the same route, whereas the kinase-domain substitution Met2327Ile confers resistance to ATP-competitive inhibitors without preventing drug docking.
edges.notes: Bivalent agents that engage the FRB and the ATP site together retain activity against these substitutions.

edges.mechanism: Vistusertib competes with ATP at the mTOR kinase cleft, inhibiting mTORC1 and mTORC2; it was selected from the AZD8055 series for improved pharmaceutical properties.

Vistusertib occupies the mTOR ATP cleft, which is common to both complexes, and therefore suppresses mTORC1 output completely, including the 4E-BP1 phosphorylation sites that allosteric agents leave only partly suppressed.

Because the ATP site is shared by both complexes and is not occluded by Rictor or mSin1, vistusertib inhibits mTORC2 as completely as mTORC1, abolishing AKT Ser473 phosphorylation; this is the source of the added metabolic toxicity of the ATP-competitive class.
edges.notes: Site is the AKT readout of mTORC2 activity.

edges.mechanism: Complete inhibition of mTORC2 by ATP-competitive agents produces hyperglycaemia through combined beta-cell dysfunction and peripheral insulin resistance, with mTORC2 contributing more than mTORC1; this metabolic ceiling limited clinical development of the class.
edges.context: class-level attribution; vistusertib-specific incidence not reported
edges.notes: Hyperglycaemia is reported across ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors; no incidence specific to vistusertib is available.

edges.mechanism: Apo-CASTOR1 sequesters GATOR2, performing for arginine the function Sestrin2 performs for leucine
CASTOR2 heterodimerises with CASTOR1; the heterodimer binds GATOR2 but CASTOR2 itself does not confer high-affinity arginine binding
CASTOR2 binds GATOR2 as part of the CASTOR1-CASTOR2 heterodimer, contributing to arginine-regulated control of the hub
GCN2 phosphorylates eIF2alpha Ser51 during amino-acid starvation, reducing global translation initiation and inducing ATF4, which transcribes SESN2 to sustain mTORC1 suppression.
LARS1 was reported to act as a leucine-dependent GAP for RagD, driving it to the GDP state that supports mTORC1 recruitment
edges.notes: Contested: the yeast orthologue acts on Gtr1, the RagA/B counterpart, with the opposite activity [51]; the mammalian and fungal models are unreconciled.

edges.mechanism: MAT2A converts methionine and ATP into S-adenosylmethionine, the metabolite bound by SAMTOR, and acute MAT2A loss attenuates methionine sensing by mTORC1 in cultured cells; MAT2A is the extrahepatic isoform, whereas MAT1A predominates in adult liver.
NPC1 associates with SLC38A9 and exports lysosomal cholesterol; loss of NPC1 traps cholesterol in the lumen and hyperactivates mTORC1 through this complex
edges.notes: The inhibitory sign reflects NPC1 removing the activating sterol; the cholesterol arm remains an emerging mechanism.

edges.mechanism: OGT O-GlcNAcylates LARS1 at Ser1042 during glucose starvation, which blocks LARS1 binding to RagD and promotes ULK1 phosphorylation of its leucine-binding site, lowering leucine-induced mTORC1 activity.
edges.notes: OGT knockdown or inhibition suppresses LARS1 O-GlcNAcylation; why glucose starvation increases this modification is unresolved. Reported by a single laboratory.

edges.mechanism: Unlike Sestrin2 and CASTOR1, apo-SAMTOR acts directly on GATOR1, promoting its activity and so inhibiting mTORC1 when SAM is low
SAMTOR engages the GATOR1-KICSTOR assembly rather than GATOR2, which is why the methionine arm bypasses the Sestrin/CASTOR hub
In the absence of leucine SAR1B binds GATOR2 and blocks its inhibition of GATOR1, keeping mTORC1 off; leucine binding to SAR1B dissociates the SAR1B-GATOR2 complex.
edges.notes: Single primary report; the leucine-sensing role of SAR1B awaits independent replication.

edges.mechanism: Leucine-bound SAR1B was reported to regulate mTORC1 activity; the downstream connection to the Rag machinery is not firmly established
edges.notes: Net effect of the SAR1B arm; the molecular step is the binding of apo-SAR1B to GATOR2, and the route from GATOR2 to the Rag GTPases was not defined in the primary report.

edges.mechanism: Sestrin1 interacts with GATOR2 in the same way as Sestrin2, contributing to negative regulation of the amino-acid sensing pathway
edges.notes: SESN1/2/3 differ in tissue expression, so which sensing mechanism dominates is expected to vary between tissues.

edges.mechanism: Sestrin1, like sestrin2, promotes AMPK activation and downstream TSC2 phosphorylation, forming the p53-dependent feedback loop that suppresses mTORC1 after genotoxic stress.
edges.notes: Whether AMPK mediates the effect of Sestrin1 on mTORC1 is disputed; later work places sestrin action primarily through GATOR2 and the Rag GTPases.

edges.mechanism: Sestrins have been reported to activate AMPK and so to inhibit mTORC1 through TSC2, a route independent of GATOR2 sequestration; the molecular basis is undefined and Sestrin2 still suppresses mTORC1 in AMPK-null cells.
edges.notes: The AMPK arm is reported rather than reproduced; the best-supported route from Sestrin2 to mTORC1 is sequestration of GATOR2.

edges.mechanism: Sestrin1/2 were reported to bind AMPK (and TSC2) and promote AMPK-mediated TSC2 phosphorylation, mediating p53-dependent mTORC1 inhibition after genotoxic stress.
edges.notes: Later work (Chantranupong 2014, Peng 2014 Cell) shows sestrins inhibit mTORC1 primarily through GATOR2 and the Rag GTPases, independently of AMPK; the physiological contribution of the AMPK route is disputed.

edges.mechanism: Apo-Sestrin2 binds GATOR2 across the WDR24 and SEH1L beta-propellers, with auxiliary contacts to MIOS, preventing GATOR2 from inhibiting GATOR1 so RagA/B remain GDP-bound and mTORC1 leaves the lysosome; leucine binding (Kd approximately 20 microM) releases GATOR2.
edges.notes: Established in vitro and structurally, while the physiological primacy of Sestrin2 as a leucine sensor is contested. Sestrin2 is itself induced by p53 and ATF4, so stress input converges on this step.

edges.mechanism: Alternative model in which Sestrin2 acts as a guanine-nucleotide dissociation inhibitor for RagA/B, locking them in the GDP state, rather than acting only by sequestering GATOR2. Published results conflict with the GATOR2-sequestration-only model.
edges.notes: Contested: the guanine-nucleotide dissociation inhibitor model and the GATOR2-sequestration model of Sestrin action are in direct conflict and have not been reconciled.

edges.mechanism: Sestrin2 binds the WDR24-SEH1L region of GATOR2; MIOS is the principal CASTOR1-binding subunit.
Sestrin3 also binds GATOR2 and negatively regulates the amino-acid sensing pathway upstream of mTORC1

SLC1A5 (ASCT2) is an obligatory sodium-dependent antiporter for glutamine; in the original model its uptake supplies the intracellular glutamine that LAT1 effluxes to drive leucine import, although later work finds ASCT2 dispensable for glutamine accumulation and mTORC1 activation when SNAT1 and SNAT2 are expressed.
edges.notes: The transport step itself is firmly established; the role of ASCT2 as the driver of leucine-dependent mTORC1 activation is disputed.

edges.mechanism: Arginine-activated SLC38A9 effluxes essential amino acids from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol, which is how protein taken up by macropinocytosis or autophagy becomes usable nutrient; loss of SLC38A9 traps these amino acids in the lysosome.
edges.notes: Lysosomal efflux through SLC38A9 is well supported, but its quantitative weight relative to cytosolic amino-acid sensing is undefined.

edges.mechanism: SLC38A9 effluxes leucine and other essential amino acids from the lysosomal lumen in an arginine-dependent manner, supplying the cytosolic pool read by Sestrin2
edges.notes: Lysosomal leucine efflux through SLC38A9 is well supported; its quantitative weight relative to cytosolic sensing is undefined.

edges.mechanism: Node-level summary: SLC38A9 activates mTORC1 through luminal arginine sensing and through lysosomal efflux of leucine and other essential amino acids; the cholesterol-sensing arm it shares with NPC1 is less firmly established and is carried separately.
edges.notes: Established for the arginine-sensing and transport arms; the cholesterol arm is emerging.

edges.mechanism: SLC38A9 and NPC1 physically associate in the lysosomal cholesterol-sensing pathway. This binding edge does not assert inhibition of NPC1 transport by SLC38A9.
edges.notes: Reciprocal arm of the SLC38A9-NPC1 cholesterol switch; the cholesterol route is less firmly established than arginine sensing.

edges.mechanism: SLC38A9 co-assembles with Ragulator and the Rag GTPases as part of the lysosomal amino-acid sensing machinery; this contact positions the transceptor, while the arginine-dependent activating signal is exerted on the Rag GTPases.
Arginine-bound SLC38A9 binds the Rag-Ragulator complex and signals amino-acid sufficiency, promoting mTORC1 recruitment
SLC38A9 acts as a non-canonical GEF for RagA, accelerating GDP release and favouring the GTP-loaded, Raptor-binding state
edges.notes: Non-canonical exchange mechanism; the activity resides in the N-terminal Ram domain of SLC38A9.

edges.mechanism: SLC3A2 (4F2hc/CD98 heavy chain) is disulphide-bonded to the SLC7A5 light chain; the heavy chain is required for surface delivery and transport function of the LAT1 heterodimer.
edges.notes: The heavy chain is transport-inactive on its own and acts as the trafficking subunit; SLC7A5 carries the transport site.

edges.mechanism: LAT1/4F2hc is an obligatory antiporter: it effluxes intracellular glutamine in exchange for extracellular leucine, so SLC1A5-mediated glutamine uptake is the driving force for leucine import. This coupling is why glutamine deprivation blunts leucine-driven mTORC1 activation.
edges.notes: Obligatory antiport: leucine import is coupled to glutamine efflux, so this route depletes rather than supplies the cytosolic glutamine pool, which is why glutamine deprivation blunts leucine-driven mTORC1 activation.

edges.mechanism: LAT1 imports leucine at the plasma membrane in obligatory exchange for efflux of intracellular glutamine, setting the cytosolic leucine concentration seen by the sensors
edges.notes: Leucine import through LAT1 is obligatorily coupled to efflux of intracellular glutamine.

edges.mechanism: The proton gradient generated by the v-ATPase drives amino-acid efflux from the lysosomal lumen; lysosomal metabolomics shows v-ATPase- and mTOR-dependent control of lysosomal amino-acid export, placing the pump upstream of SLC38A9-dependent efflux as well as of the inside-out Ragulator signal.
edges.notes: Transport-level role of the v-ATPase, distinct from its inside-out signalling to Ragulator.

edges.mechanism: The v-ATPase relays luminal amino-acid content outward by regulating Ragulator GEF activity toward RagA/B - the inside-out sensing mechanism
v-ATPase function is required for amino acids to drive the Rag heterodimer into its active nucleotide configuration and recruit mTORC1
Androgen/AR signalling raises mTORC1 activity and cyclin D translation in prostate cancer cells; AR and PI3K–AKT are reciprocally cross-inhibitory in PTEN-null prostate cancer.
edges.notes: Indirect, multi-step input; the molecular intermediary (PI3K-dependent and -independent components) is not fully resolved.

edges.mechanism: Indirect. EGFR carries no high-affinity p85-binding motif of its own, so EGF-stimulated PI3K and AKT signalling is relayed through the docking protein GAB1 and, in EGFR-ERBB3 heterodimers, through the pYXXM motifs of ERBB3.
edges.notes: this is the route by which receptor tyrosine kinase amplification raises PI3K flux.

edges.mechanism: Non-genomic: ligand-bound ERα binds p85α and activates PI3K–AKT; in TSC2-null cells estrogen enhances survival and pulmonary metastasis via ERK/mTORC1 signalling.
edges.notes: Cell-type dependent; the LAM relevance is the reason this input is documented in the mTOR literature.

edges.mechanism: IGF-1R kinase tyrosine-phosphorylates IRS-1 (and IRS-2) YXXM motifs, recruiting p85–PI3K; mechanistically parallel to INSR.
Activated INSR kinase phosphorylates IRS-1 on multiple tyrosines in YXXM motifs, generating SH2-docking sites for p85–PI3K and GRB2.
edges.notes: Tyrosine sites are numerous (e.g. human Tyr612/Tyr632 equivalents of rat Tyr608/Tyr628 bind p85); not listed individually to avoid numbering ambiguity.

edges.mechanism: Phospho-YXXM motifs on IRS-1 engage the SH2 domains of p85, relieving p85 inhibition of p110 and bringing PI3K to membrane PI(4,5)P2.

Indirect effect: insulin signalling through IRS-1, PI3K and AKT is a required positive input to hepatic SREBP1c expression and processing. In liver-specific Tsc1-deficient mice, S6K1-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation of IRS-1 suppresses this input and SREBP1c, protecting against diet-induced steatosis despite constitutive mTORC1 activity.
edges.notes: Genetic activation of hepatic mTORC1 and its pharmacological inhibition are therefore not mirror images for liver lipid phenotypes.

edges.mechanism: Neurofibromin's GAP-related domain accelerates Ras GTP hydrolysis; NF1 loss raises Ras·GTP and ERK/RSK input to TSC2 and Raptor.

Phosphatidic acid binds the mTOR FRB domain, the surface also engaged by the FKBP12-rapamycin complex, and stimulates mTORC1; the Arg2109 dependence rests on mutagenesis in the original report, and displacement of DEPTOR has been described by one group.
edges.notes: Mechanical activation of this route is ERK-independent. The quantitative contribution of phosphatidic acid relative to the other mechanical inputs to mTORC1 is unresolved.

edges.mechanism: Phospholipase D-generated phosphatidic acid transmits mechanical activation to mTOR, by an ERK-independent mechanism consistent with direct activation.
PA is reported to be required for assembly/stability of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 and to oppose rapamycin at the FRB domain.
Class I PI3K phosphorylates the 3-OH of PI(4,5)P2 to generate PI(3,4,5)P3 at the plasma membrane.
Class I PI3K, activated by receptor tyrosine kinase engagement, converts PIP2 to PIP3.

Growth-factor signalling through PI3K has been reported to promote association of mTORC2 with the ribosome as an activating input; this step comes from a single line of work, while the reproduced growth-factor input is direct PIP3 binding to the mSin1 PH domain, which relieves autoinhibition and recruits the complex to the membrane.
edges.notes: Upstream control of mTORC2 beyond PIP3 binding and ribosome association remains poorly resolved.

edges.mechanism: p85 nSH2 and iSH2 contact the p110α helical and C2 domains to restrain basal lipid-kinase activity; pY-peptide binding to nSH2 releases this (the contacts disrupted by E545K/H1047R).
p85α (nSH2–iSH2–cSH2) constitutively binds the p110 adaptor-binding domain, stabilising the catalytic subunit and forming the class IA heterodimer.
PI(4,5)P2 is 3-phosphorylated by PI3K to PI(3,4,5)P3; the reaction is reversed by the 3-phosphatase PTEN.
PIP3 (and PI(3,4)P2) binding to the AKT PH domain recruits AKT to the membrane and relieves PH–kinase autoinhibition, exposing Thr308 to PDK1.
PIP3 recruits AKT to the plasma membrane through its PH domain, which is prerequisite for both Thr308 and Ser473 phosphorylation.
PIP3 binding to the mSin1 C-terminal PH domain relieves its autoinhibitory fold-back onto mTOR and recruits mTORC2 to the plasma membrane where AKT resides.
The C-terminal PH domain of mSin1 binds PIP3, which releases the PH domain from mTOR and derepresses the kinase.
edges.notes: PIP3-dependent relief of mSin1 autoinhibition is reproduced across laboratories.

edges.mechanism: PIP3 binds the mSin1 PH domain and releases it from mTOR, relieving autoinhibition of the kinase.
edges.notes: Reproduced across laboratories; the best-supported upstream input to mTORC2.

edges.mechanism: The PDK1 PH domain binds PIP3 and PI(3,4)P2, holding PDK1 at the plasma membrane where PIP3-recruited AKT becomes accessible. PDK1 is catalytically active without stimulation and its own distribution changes little on growth-factor treatment, so the lipid governs substrate access, although phosphoinositide binding also promotes PDK1 trans-autophosphorylation.
PIP3 binding by mSin1 simultaneously relieves autoinhibition and recruits mTORC2 to the plasma membrane, co-localising it with membrane-targeted AKT.
PIP3 binding simultaneously recruits mTORC2 to the plasma membrane, co-localising it with its membrane-targeted substrate AKT.

PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 generated by PI3K binds the mSin1 PH domain and pulls it off the kinase domain, relieving autoinhibition and simultaneously anchoring mTORC2 at the plasma membrane where Akt is recruited.
PLD1 hydrolyses phosphatidylcholine to phosphatidic acid and choline.
PTEN 3-phosphatase hydrolyses PIP3 back to PI(4,5)P2, terminating PDK1/AKT membrane recruitment; the dominant negative regulator of the PI3K–AKT–mTORC1 axis.
PTEN dephosphorylates PIP3 to PIP2, terminating the lipid signal that relieves mSin1 autoinhibition and recruits mTORC2 and AKT.

GTP-bound H-Ras and K-Ras (predominantly KRAS4A) bind the atypical Ras-binding domain of mSin1. Oncogenic Ras was reported to promote mTORC2 activity at the plasma membrane, but a Sin1 mutant unable to bind Ras supports normal mTORC2 assembly and activity in cells and mice, and Sin1 overexpression was reported to suppress Ras signalling.
edges.context: shown chiefly with oncogenic KRAS/HRAS in cultured cells
edges.notes: The consequence of Ras binding for mTORC2 activity is disputed between laboratories. The Ras-binding domain is one of the defined mSin1 regions, but no function has been firmly assigned to it.

edges.mechanism: GTP-bound H-Ras and K-Ras (predominantly KRAS4A) bind the atypical Ras-binding domain of mSin1. Oncogenic Ras was reported to promote mTORC2 activity at the plasma membrane, but a Sin1 mutant unable to bind Ras supports normal mTORC2 assembly and activity in cells and mice, and Sin1 overexpression was reported to suppress Ras signalling.
edges.notes: The consequence of Ras binding for mTORC2 activity is disputed between laboratories. The Ras-binding domain is one of the defined mSin1 regions, but no function has been firmly assigned to it.

edges.mechanism: Ras·GTP binds the p110α Ras-binding domain, allosterically activating PI3K and coupling RTK/Ras signalling to PIP3 production.
Ras·GTP binds the RAF Ras-binding and cysteine-rich domains, recruiting RAF to the membrane where dimerisation and phosphorylation activate it.

Receptor autophosphorylation creates phosphotyrosine docking sites bound by the GRB2 SH2 domain (directly on EGFR; via SHC or IRS-1 for the insulin and IGF-1 receptors), bringing the GRB2–SOS1 complex to the membrane.
Ligand-activated RTKs autophosphorylate; pYXXM sites (directly or via IRS/GAB adaptors) recruit p85–p110 to the membrane, activating class I PI3K.
edges.notes: Receptor tyrosine kinase engagement activates PI3K [72,260,386]; RTK amplification converges on PI3K [375,624].

edges.mechanism: FBP-unoccupied aldolase alters v-ATPase-Ragulator conformation, permitting AXIN-LKB1 docking and lysosomal AMPK Thr172 phosphorylation without an AMP rise; FBP-bound aldolase blocks the assembly.
edges.notes: The sensed ligand is fructose-1,6-bisphosphate; the signal starts when it dissociates from aldolase as glucose falls. Reported mainly by one laboratory, which later showed that TRPV channels relay the aldolase signal (Li et al. 2019).

edges.mechanism: AMP binding to the AMPK gamma subunit drives AXIN to tether LKB1 to AMPK, and under glucose starvation the AXIN-LKB1-AMPK complex docks on the lysosomal v-ATPase-Ragulator, allowing LKB1 to phosphorylate AMPK Thr172.
edges.notes: AXIN1 is a scaffold and does not itself phosphorylate Thr172. Evidence comes mainly from one laboratory.

edges.mechanism: Under low energy, AMP-bound AMPK, AXIN and LKB1 assemble into a complex in which AXIN tethers LKB1 to AMPK, enhancing Thr172 phosphorylation; AXIN knockdown in mouse liver impairs AMPK activation after starvation.
MO25-alpha (or MO25-beta) is the scaffold subunit of the LKB1 heterotrimer.
MO25-alpha binds the STRADA C-terminal WEF motif and the LKB1 kinase domain, stabilising the heterotrimer and increasing LKB1 activity about 10-fold beyond STRADA alone.
CaMKK-beta phosphorylates AMPK Thr172 in response to rises in cytosolic Ca2+ (e.g. ionophores, hormones), independently of LKB1 and without a change in AMP:ATP.

In normoxia PHD2 hydroxylates HIF-1α at Pro402 and Pro564 using O2 as co-substrate, creating the pVHL-binding degron; the reaction rate is limited by oxygen tension, which is what makes HIF-1α an oxygen sensor.
edges.notes: Pro402 and Pro564 lie in two independent oxygen-dependent degradation domains, each of which recruits pVHL once hydroxylated; PHD1 and PHD3 can hydroxylate the same residues.

edges.mechanism: PERK phosphorylates eIF2alpha Ser51, trapping eIF2B and reducing ternary-complex formation; global initiation falls while ATF4 translation rises.

The constitutively active LKB1–STRADα–MO25 heterotrimer is the upstream kinase that phosphorylates the AMPK activation loop at Thr172; STRADα and MO25 are required for LKB1 catalytic competence and cytoplasmic localisation.
edges.notes: The LKB1-STRADalpha-MO25 heterotrimer is the physiological AMPK kinase; STRADalpha and MO25 are required for LKB1 catalytic competence and cytoplasmic localisation.

edges.mechanism: Complex I oxidises NADH and pumps protons, sustaining the proton-motive force that ATP synthase uses, so complex I activity is required for maximal oxidative ATP production rather than converting a substrate into ATP. Biguanide inhibition of complex I therefore lowers ATP and raises AMP and ADP, the classical high-dose route to AMPK activation.

Metformin-bound PEN2 binds the v-ATPase accessory subunit ATP6AP1 and inhibits the lysosomal v-ATPase, triggering AXIN–LKB1-dependent activation of lysosomal AMPK at clinically relevant metformin concentrations and without a fall in cellular ATP.
edges.notes: Completes the low-dose metformin route from PEN2 through v-ATPase inhibition to lysosomal AMPK activation; reported by a single laboratory (Ma T et al., Nature 2022;603:159-165).

edges.mechanism: PEX5, the peroxisomal targeting-signal receptor, binds TSC2 and localises a pool of the TSC complex to the peroxisome, where it suppresses Rheb in response to reactive oxygen species; TSC1 is recognised by the partner receptor PEX19.
edges.notes: Pathogenic TSC2 mutations reduce PEX5 binding and abolish peroxisomal localisation, Rheb-GAP activity and reactive-oxygen-species-dependent suppression of mTORC1; reported by a single laboratory.

edges.mechanism: LKB1 (with STRADA/MO25) phosphorylates the AMPK alpha activation-loop Thr172; AMP bound to the gamma subunit makes AMPK a better substrate and protects pThr172, so net phosphorylation rises with AMP/ATP.
edges.notes: LKB1 is constitutively active; regulation is at the substrate (AMPK) level.

edges.mechanism: LKB1 is the catalytic subunit of the LKB1-STRADA-MO25 heterotrimer, the constitutively active upstream kinase of AMPK.
STRAD-alpha (or STRAD-beta) is the pseudokinase subunit of the LKB1 heterotrimer required for its activity and cytoplasmic localisation.

The pseudokinase STRAD-alpha binds the LKB1 kinase domain and, together with MO25, stabilises the catalytically active conformation and anchors LKB1 in the cytoplasm where AMPK is phosphorylated; STRAD-alpha alone gives only partial activation.
edges.notes: Reported activation of LKB1 refers to the LKB1-STRADalpha-MO25 heterotrimer rather than to STRADalpha binding alone.

edges.mechanism: Glutaminase hydrolyses glutamine to glutamate and ammonia, the first step of glutaminolysis; glutamate is then converted to alpha-ketoglutarate by GLUD1 or transaminases, so GLS is required for, but does not itself produce, alpha-ketoglutarate from glutamine.
edges.notes: Blocking glutaminolysis was reported to prevent RagB GTP loading and mTORC1 activation by glutamine and leucine (Duran 2012); that downstream link rests on one laboratory.

edges.mechanism: Glutaminase converts glutamine to glutamate, the entry step that permits GDH-dependent anaplerosis
Loss of neurofibromin removes Ras-GAP activity, raising Ras·GTP and MAPK/RSK input to TSC2 and Raptor.
edges.notes: Neurofibromin is a Ras-GAP; its loss raises Ras-GTP and increases ERK and RSK input to the TSC complex and Raptor.

edges.mechanism: Loss of NF1 is listed among the recurrent alterations in the PI3K-AKT-mTOR landscape in cancer.
Loss of the Ras GAP neurofibromin raises RAS-ERK-RSK signalling, which converges on the TSC complex and so raises mTORC1 output.
Helical-domain mutations escape p85 nSH2 inhibition; kinase-domain H1047R increases membrane binding; both raise PIP3 and AKT–mTORC1 flux (distal-network lesion).
edges.context: breast (30–40%), endometrial (30%) cancer; somatic mosaic in FCD II/HME
edges.notes: A distal-network lesion: mTORC1 is only one effector among several, so this is a poor predictor of rapalog benefit (BOLERO-2 benefit was independent of PIK3CA genotype).

edges.mechanism: Helical (E542K, E545K) and kinase (H1047R/L) hotspot mutations raise PI3K catalytic output and hence PIP3 production.
edges.context: somatic; also mosaic in cortical malformation

edges.mechanism: Activating PIK3CA mutations are present in roughly 30-40% of breast cancers and define the population in which alpelisib improved progression-free survival.
Activating PIK3CA mutations occur in roughly 30% of endometrial cancers; a PTEN- and PIK3CA-altered endometrial cancer gave the first complete response to RMC-5552.
Somatic mosaic PIK3CA activation is an alternative genotype of focal cortical dysplasia type II, converging on the same mTORC1 hyperactivation.
edges.context: somatic mosaicism restricted to dysplastic cortex

edges.mechanism: Hemimegalencephaly is caused by de novo somatic mutations in components of the PI3K-AKT3-mTOR pathway, including PIK3CA.

Mosaic somatic PIK3CA activating variants cause the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (CLOVES, megalencephaly-capillary malformation, isolated macrodactyly), the non-neoplastic counterpart of the somatic mosaicism described for FCD type II and hemimegalencephaly.
PIK3CA mutation raises flux into a branched network in which mTORC1 is one effector among several, the defining property of the distal-network class.
PIK3CA hotspot mutation was the prospective selection criterion in SOLAR-1 and predicts benefit, in contrast to its failure to predict rapalog benefit in the same disease.
PTEN loss removes PIP3 hydrolysis and raises AKT activity; it is a frequent distal-network lesion in prostate, glioblastoma and endometrial cancer.
edges.notes: The commonly quoted prevalence figures for PTEN loss require a primary epidemiological source before they are restated.

edges.mechanism: Loss-of-function PTEN alterations are among the most common lesions of prostate cancer, glioblastoma and endometrial carcinoma, and raise flux through the PI3K-AKT network without creating dependency on the mTOR node.

PTEN is one of the most frequently mutated genes in endometrioid endometrial carcinoma, and a patient with PTEN- and PIK3CA-altered endometrial cancer had a complete response to the mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-5552 that was ongoing beyond six months.
PTEN is one of the most frequently inactivated tumour suppressors in glioblastoma, where loss-of-function mutations and deletions are common.
Germline PTEN loss causes the PTEN hamartoma tumour syndromes, including Cowden syndrome, with hamartomas, macrocephaly and elevated breast, thyroid and endometrial cancer risk.
edges.notes: Well-established link, supported by the primary literature.

edges.mechanism: PTEN is frequently inactivated in prostate cancer through mutation or deletion, raising flux through the PI3K-AKT pathway.
Loss of the PIP3 3-phosphatase PTEN allows PIP3 to accumulate, raising flux through PDK1 and AKT into the branched distal network.
PTEN loss raises network flux while AKT retains mTORC1-independent output to GSK3beta, FOXO and MDM2, so no mTOR-node dependency is created.
Receptor tyrosine kinase gene amplification increases ligand-dependent and -independent PI3K recruitment; distal-network lesion converging on PI3K.
Receptor tyrosine kinase amplification converges on PI3K, raising network flux without creating dependency on the mTOR node specifically.
Receptor tyrosine kinase amplification converges on PI3K and belongs among the distal-network alterations.
Everolimus is an ABCB1 (P-glycoprotein) substrate; brain accumulation is restricted by ABCB1 and rises when the transporter is absent or pharmacologically inhibited.
Everolimus is an ABCB1 substrate; brain accumulation is restricted by the transporter and rises when it is absent or pharmacologically inhibited.
Sirolimus and everolimus are ABCB1 substrates; brain accumulation of everolimus rises when the transporter is absent or pharmacologically inhibited.
edges.notes: Shields CNS from systemic exposure but limits efficacy wherever CNS target engagement is the object.

edges.mechanism: Efflux at the blood-brain barrier shields the CNS from systemic exposure but equally limits target engagement wherever the brain is the therapeutic object, decoupling central from peripheral exposure.
edges.notes: A dose titrated to a peripheral marker such as whole-blood S6K1 phosphorylation is not thereby titrated in brain.

edges.mechanism: Sirolimus is an ABCB1 substrate, so central and peripheral exposure-response relationships cannot be assumed to coincide; a dose titrated to whole-blood S6K1 phosphorylation is not thereby titrated in brain.

P-glycoprotein effluxes sirolimus at the apical membrane of enterocytes, which together with first-pass CYP3A metabolism keeps oral bioavailability low: approximately 14% for the oral solution, with tablet exposure about 27% higher and not bioequivalent to it. The same transporter handling underlies the extensive drug-interaction profile of the drug.

Temsirolimus and the sirolimus it yields are P-glycoprotein substrates, so efflux limits their distribution into tissues, most consequentially across the blood-brain barrier. Because temsirolimus is administered intravenously, intestinal efflux does not contribute to its systemic exposure.
Everolimus is likewise a CYP3A4 substrate, giving extensive interaction potential with azoles, macrolides, rifampicin and anticonvulsants and requiring exposure-guided dosing.

In mice, CYP3A acts together with plasma carboxylesterase to clear everolimus systemically and so sets the blood concentration from which central exposure derives; restriction of brain penetration itself is attributed chiefly to P-glycoprotein at the blood-brain barrier.

CYP3A4 in gut and liver demethylates and hydroxylates sirolimus, so CYP3A4 inducers and inhibitors shift its exposure several-fold; whole-blood trough monitoring, commonly in the range of 5-15 ng/mL in transplantation, is therefore standard.

Temsirolimus is cleared principally by hepatic CYP3A4, which hydroxylates and demethylates it, so CYP3A4 inhibitors and inducers markedly alter its exposure. The drug is given intravenously, so no intestinal first-pass step contributes, and its principal active metabolite sirolimus arises by hydrolysis of the temsirolimus ester rather than by CYP3A4.
