edges.notes: The MK2 route rests on a single study; independent work shows that mTOR also sustains the SASP by promoting IL1A translation.

edges.mechanism: Microglial Tsc1 deletion is accompanied by astrocyte proliferation and severe early-onset spontaneous recurrent seizures, without a pro-inflammatory cytokine signature.
Chronic mTORC1 hyperactivation initially expands beta-cell mass and secretion but leads to dedifferentiation and failure through ER stress and suppressed autophagy.
Beta-cell-specific Raptor deletion impairs beta-cell mass and functional maturation.
Cardiac mTORC1 supports physiological hypertrophy, yet sustained activity contributes to maladaptive remodelling, which partial inhibition attenuates in multiple models.
edges.notes: Non-monotonic: both insufficient and sustained activity are deleterious.

edges.mechanism: Adipocyte Raptor-null mice are lean with enhanced mitochondrial respiration, so adipose mTORC1 supports fat accumulation.
Intracerebroventricular leucine raises hypothalamic S6K1 phosphorylation and suppresses food intake and body weight; rapamycin abolishes the effect.
edges.notes: Established in rodents; no human study separates central from peripheral contribution.

edges.mechanism: SREBP1c-dependent lipogenesis driven by hepatic mTORC1 contributes to steatosis when insulin is chronically elevated.
edges.notes: Hepatic mTORC1 is required for insulin-induced SREBP1c and lipogenesis, but mTORC1 activation alone is not sufficient: liver Tsc1 deletion lowers Akt signalling and protects against diet-induced steatosis, so intact Akt signalling, which also suppresses Insig2a, is required alongside it.

edges.mechanism: Chronic mTORC1 activation in obesity drives insulin resistance through S6K1-IRS-1 feedback and through lipotoxicity from constrained adipose storage capacity.
Reduced TOR signalling extends lifespan in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Caenorhabditis elegans and Drosophila melanogaster, so TOR activity limits lifespan.

Sustained mTORC1 activity contributes to maladaptive cardiac remodelling, in contrast to the physiological hypertrophy the same complex supports, and partial inhibition attenuates pathological hypertrophy in several models.
edges.notes: Cardiac mTOR also has protective roles, including after ischaemic injury, so the maladaptive arm is dose- and context-dependent rather than a uniform property of mTORC1 activity.

edges.mechanism: Microglial Tsc1 loss produces an amoeboid, highly proliferative and phagocytic phenotype without a pro-inflammatory cytokine signature, with reduced synapse density.

Muscle-specific Raptor deletion produces progressive dystrophy, impaired oxidative capacity and shortened lifespan, so intact mTORC1 restrains the dystrophic phenotype; muscle-specific Rictor deletion is close to phenotypically silent.

mTORC1 activity is required for load-induced hypertrophy: rapamycin blocks the hypertrophic response to IGF-1, mechanical overload and chronic stimulation. Sustained mTORC1 activation is not by itself sufficient, since constitutive activation by Tsc1 deletion in muscle fails to produce hypertrophy and instead causes a late-onset myopathy with blocked autophagy.
Oligodendrocyte-lineage Raptor loss delays myelination onset and produces persistent hypomyelination with reduced sheath thickness, regionally worse in spinal cord.
edges.notes: Established in rodents; effect of chronic low-dose inhibition on adult human white matter unresolved.

edges.mechanism: Podocytes require a calibrated level of mTORC1 activity: Raptor deletion in podocytes causes injury and proteinuria, while podocyte Tsc1 deletion causes proteinuric glomerulosclerosis, so both insufficient and excessive activity damage the filtration barrier.
edges.notes: Both limbs matter clinically: mTOR inhibitors themselves can cause proteinuria, while podocyte mTORC1 activation drives the glomerular lesion of diabetic nephropathy in mice.

edges.mechanism: Microglia-restricted Tsc1 deletion reduces synapse density alongside an amoeboid, highly proliferative and phagocytic microglial phenotype; the effect of pathway hyperactivation on synapses is therefore not cell-autonomous to neurons.
edges.notes: both are needed.

edges.mechanism: Rheb-mTORC1 is required for Th1 and Th17 differentiation; T cell-specific mTOR deletion abrogates Th1, Th2 and Th17 differentiation altogether.

In naive mouse CD4 cells without exogenous TGF-beta, combined inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2 promotes Foxp3 induction while inhibition of either complex alone is insufficient; established regulatory T cells conversely require mTORC1 for their metabolic programme and suppressive function.
edges.context: de novo Treg differentiation in vitro; not mature Treg expansion
edges.notes: Differentiation, expansion and suppressive function are distinct endpoints; mature Tregs require mTORC1 for normal function.

edges.mechanism: Adipocyte-specific Raptor deletion impairs adipogenesis and reduces fat mass with enhanced mitochondrial respiration
Beta-cell-specific Raptor deletion impairs beta-cell mass, functional maturation and insulin processing.
mTOR-dependent dendritic translation underlies the late, protein-synthesis-dependent phase of LTP

Proliferating haematopoietic progenitors require mTORC1, which accounts for the cytopenias seen during rapalog therapy. Restraint of mTORC1 by the TSC complex is conversely required to keep haematopoietic stem cells quiescent: Tsc1 deletion drives stem cells out of quiescence, increases mitochondrial biogenesis and reactive oxygen species, and impairs self-renewal, so the compartment requires calibrated rather than maximal activity.
Cardiac mTORC1 supports physiological hypertrophy; only the mTORC2 arm of the cardiomyocyte row was encoded.
In the arcuate nucleus mTORC1 operates as a nutrient sensor, which makes the hyperphagia of Smith-Kingsmore syndrome mechanistically expected rather than incidental.
edges.notes: Established in rodents and unresolved in humans, where the central and peripheral contributions have not been separated; some metabolic effects attributed to liver, adipose tissue and beta-cells may therefore be centrally mediated.

edges.mechanism: Podocyte Raptor deletion produces injury and proteinuria while Tsc1 deletion causes glomerulosclerosis: a calibrated rather than monotonic requirement.
Hepatic mTORC1 drives insulin-stimulated SREBP1c-dependent lipogenesis and restrains fasting ketogenesis.
edges.notes: Activation of hepatic mTORC1 alone is not sufficient to drive lipogenesis: liver Tsc1 deletion lowers Akt signalling and protects against diet-induced steatosis, so Akt-dependent input is required alongside mTORC1.

edges.mechanism: Pathway hyperactivation in the microglial compartment drives astrocyte proliferation and seizures, a non-neuronal contribution to the mTORopathies.

Oligodendrocyte-lineage Raptor loss delays onset of myelination and produces persistent hypomyelination with reduced sheath thickness, whereas Rictor loss has modest and largely transient effects; the requirement is regional, with spinal cord affected more than corpus callosum.
edges.context: oligodendrocyte lineage; regional (spinal cord > corpus callosum)

edges.mechanism: Rapidly renewing oral epithelium depends on mTORC1, which is why stomatitis affects roughly 30-60% of treated patients depending on indication and is substantially preventable with topical dexamethasone or tacrolimus prophylaxis.
Muscle-specific Raptor deletion produces progressive dystrophy, impaired oxidative capacity and shortened lifespan, establishing mTORC1 as the dominant complex in muscle.
Both complexes are required for the glycolytic and glutaminolytic reprogramming of effector T cell activation, so partial inhibition is the pharmacological objective.
mTORC2 phosphorylates the hydrophobic motif Ser473; AKT docks on the mSin1 CRIM domain ~75 Å from the active site. Ser473 selectively enhances activity toward FOXO1/3 and BAD over GSK3β/TSC2.
edges.notes: Recruitment of AKT through a 'tri-arginine cluster' on mSin1, common in secondary sources, lacks clear primary support; the distal-docking model rests on a single structural study [597].

edges.mechanism: Cotranslational, constitutive turn-motif phosphorylation at Thr450 by ribosome-associated mTORC2 is required for AKT folding and stability.
Ribosome-associated mTORC2 phosphorylates the turn motif of nascent AKT cotranslationally, which is required for folding and stability of the newly synthesised polypeptide.
edges.notes: This cotranslational activity is a defining output of the ribosome-associated mTORC2 pool.

edges.mechanism: mTORC2 is the hydrophobic-motif kinase for Akt: phosphorylation of Ser473 completes activation-loop-dependent activation and sets Akt substrate selectivity (notably toward FOXO).
edges.notes: AKT phosphorylated only at Thr308 retains substantial activity toward GSK3beta and TSC2, whereas Ser473 phosphorylation markedly enhances activity toward FOXO1, FOXO3a and BAD.

edges.mechanism: Turn-motif phosphorylation at Thr450 is constitutive and occurs cotranslationally on ribosome-associated mTORC2; it is required for folding and stability of nascent AKT.
edges.notes: Phospho-Thr450 is also read by the mSin1 CRIM docking surface, coupling stability to the Ser473 proofreading step [597].

edges.mechanism: mTORC2 is the hydrophobic-motif (PDK2) kinase for AKT; with PDK1-mediated Thr308 it gives full AKT activity.
edges.notes: Identification of mTORC2 as the long-sought PDK2 resolved more than a decade of uncertainty.

edges.mechanism: DEPTOR is phosphorylated by mTORC2 as well as mTORC1, which likewise promotes its degradation and relieves inhibition of the complex.
Active mTOR phosphorylates its own inhibitory subunit DEPTOR, marking it for degradation — a self-amplifying loop in which active mTOR removes its own brake.
mTORC2 supports PKC maturation by priming selected isoforms; subsequent hydrophobic-motif phosphorylation can be autophosphorylation.
mTORC2 primes selected PKC isoforms for maturation; PDK1 phosphorylation and hydrophobic-motif autophosphorylation follow.
Control of the actin cytoskeleton was the founding mTORC2 phenotype, defined by the rapamycin-insensitive, raptor-independent Rictor–mTOR complex.
Ser473 phosphorylation markedly enhances AKT activity toward BAD, biasing mTORC2 output toward survival signalling.
edges.notes: Ser473-dependent substrate selectivity has been demonstrated for FOXO1 and FOXO3a in cells lacking mTORC2 components; its extension to BAD is inferred rather than directly shown.

edges.mechanism: Loss of mTORC2 in beta-cells lowers AKT Ser473 phosphorylation and permits nuclear FOXO1 accumulation, with a consequent rise in p27 protein and reduced beta-cell mass; the step is indirect and was scored at the protein level.
edges.notes: Transcriptional and post-translational routes to p27 accumulation were not distinguished.

edges.mechanism: Beta-cell Rictor deletion elevates p27, contributing to the imbalance between beta-cell proliferation and cell size.
By supplying Ser473, mTORC2 biases AKT output toward survival and transcriptional programmes (FOXO, BAD) rather than toward its metabolic substrates.

Ser473 phosphorylation is substrate-selective rather than globally activating: AKT phosphorylated only at Thr308 retains substantial activity toward GSK3-beta and TSC2, whereas Ser473 markedly enhances activity toward FOXO1. mTORC2 therefore specifically suppresses FOXO1.
edges.notes: Ref [204] (Guertin 2006) is titled 'mTORC2 is required for signaling to Akt-FOXO' and is direct support.

edges.mechanism: Beta-cell Rictor deletion reduces AKT Ser473 phosphorylation and produces nuclear FOXO1 accumulation.
Ser473 phosphorylation markedly enhances AKT activity toward FOXO3a, so mTORC2 loss de-represses FOXO3a-dependent transcription.
Hepatic mTORC2 supports glycolysis through AKT-dependent glucokinase expression.
Hepatic mTORC2, acting through AKT-mediated FOXO1 suppression, restrains gluconeogenesis; liver-specific Rictor deletion produces glucose intolerance.
edges.notes: Opposite in sign to hepatic mTORC1 output, which is the basis of the complex-divergence argument for liver.

edges.mechanism: Hepatic mTORC2 acts through AKT-mediated FOXO1 suppression to restrain gluconeogenesis; the complexes therefore act in opposite directions on hepatic glucose output.
Adipocyte Rictor deletion reduces insulin-stimulated glucose uptake; mTORC2 output through AKT is the limiting arm.
Adipocyte Rictor deletion reduces insulin-stimulated glucose uptake while altering lipid handling and body growth.

The intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of mTOR within mTORC2 has been reported to phosphorylate and activate the type I IGF receptor and the insulin receptor, constituting a feed-forward arm from mTORC2 back onto the receptor tier that would amplify PI3K-PIP3 input to mTORC2 itself.
edges.notes: Graded emerging: the claim that mTOR has tyrosine kinase activity is not independently replicated as widely as the serine/threonine activity and should not be presented as settled.

edges.mechanism: Insulin secretion and beta-cell survival depend on mTORC2 in the islet, so both complexes are required there, unlike the opposing arrangement in liver and adipose tissue; reduced insulin output contributes to the dysglycaemia seen at immunosuppressive exposures of mTOR inhibitors.
edges.notes: Beta-cell Rictor deletion principally reduces beta-cell mass and proliferation, and the fall in insulin output has not been dissociated from that loss of mass.

edges.mechanism: Lipolysis and insulin-stimulated glucose uptake are the adipose outputs that depend on mTORC2; adipocyte Rictor deletion alters lipid handling, and pharmacological inhibition is expected to produce altered lipid handling and hypertriglyceridaemia.
Forebrain Rictor deletion selectively impairs L-LTP while leaving early-phase LTP intact; mTORC1 supports the translational component, mTORC2 the structural one.
edges.notes: Reproduced across laboratories.

edges.mechanism: Forebrain Rictor deletion selectively impairs L-LTP while sparing early-phase LTP; the mechanism is Tiam1-Rac1-dependent actin polymerisation, not translational control.
A distinct mTORC2–AKT pool resides at ER–mitochondria contact sites and controls MAM integrity, Ca2+ transfer and mitochondrial physiology.
edges.notes: Reported by a single laboratory and not independently replicated.

edges.mechanism: Adipose mTORC2 drives ChREBP-dependent de novo lipogenesis, with consequences for hepatic glucose metabolism.
Adipose-tissue mTORC2 regulates ChREBP-driven de novo lipogenesis, with consequences for hepatic glucose metabolism.

mTOR autophosphorylates at Ser2481 within the assembled complex; in mTORC2 this autophosphorylation is a complex-specific readout of intrinsic catalytic activity and is rapamycin-insensitive under acute treatment, unlike the mTORC1-associated pool.
edges.notes: Ser2481 is an activity-associated readout; the cited study does not establish that phosphorylation at this site activates mTOR.

edges.mechanism: Oligodendrocyte-lineage Rictor deletion has modest and largely transient effects on myelination, whereas Raptor loss causes persistent hypomyelination; only the raptor/rictor double mutant impairs oligodendrocyte differentiation itself, indicating that mTORC2 contributes but is not rate-limiting while mTORC1 remains intact.
edges.context: rodent; regional - spinal cord affected more than corpus callosum
edges.notes: Effect is 'modulates', not 'required_for': the cited work shows mTORC2 is explicitly NOT rate-limiting. Encoding this as a requirement would misrepresent the source.

edges.mechanism: A small molecule that raises mTORC2 activity reverses age-associated long-term memory impairment in aged mice and flies, and enhancing mTORC2-dependent actin polymerisation likewise improves long-term memory.
edges.notes: Pharmacological gain-of-function evidence from a single report in mice and flies, with no independent replication and no human data.

edges.mechanism: mTORC2 in adipose tissue negatively controls whole-body growth, so adipocyte Rictor deletion increases body size - a direction of effect opposite to the usual anabolic framing of the pathway.
edges.notes: Ref [126] (Cybulski 2009) is titled 'mTOR complex 2 in adipose tissue negatively controls whole-body growth'.

edges.mechanism: Adipose-specific Rictor deletion increases whole-body growth, so adipose mTORC2 negatively controls somatic growth.
Loss of mTORC2 removes AKT-dependent FOXO1 suppression and insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, producing glucose intolerance and peripheral insulin resistance.
Loss of hepatic mTORC2 disinhibits gluconeogenesis and reduces glucokinase-dependent glycolysis, producing glucose intolerance; this is the chief source of rapalog dysglycaemia.
Renal mTORC2 loss causes salt wasting and hypotension through failure of SGK1-dependent activation of ENaC, the Na+/K+-ATPase and CLC-K in the distal nephron.

Chronic mTORC2 loss produces peripheral insulin resistance, which is distinct from direct beta-cell toxicity; the two together account for new-onset diabetes after transplantation at immunosuppressive exposures.
Chronic mTORC2 loss produces peripheral insulin resistance, the second mechanistic arm of rapalog-associated diabetes alongside direct beta-cell toxicity.
edges.context: peripheral tissues under chronic rapalog exposure

edges.mechanism: Conditional Rictor deletion in the postnatal murine forebrain selectively impairs long-term memory while sparing short-term memory; conversely, a compound that raises mTORC2 activity converts early-phase into late-phase potentiation, enhances long-term memory in wild-type animals and reverses age-associated memory impairment in mice and flies.
edges.notes: The requirement is bidirectional and pharmacologically accessible, which is what underlies concern about cognitive effects of inhibitors that reach mTORC2.

edges.mechanism: Renal mTORC2 loss abolishes SGK1-dependent ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase regulation, causing salt wasting and hypotension.
mTORC2 phosphorylates SGK1 at Ser422, which controls ENaC, the Na+/K+-ATPase, CLC-K and NDRG1; renal mTORC2 loss causes salt wasting and hypotension.
Spine density falls when forebrain mTORC2 activity and Tiam1–Rac1-dependent actin polymerisation are reduced.
Spine density falls when forebrain mTORC2 activity is reduced, consistent with an actin-dependent structural mechanism.
A PIP3-gated pool of mTORC2 operates at the plasma membrane, where AKT is recruited by the same lipid.
mTORC2-dependent priming supports maturation of this PKC isoform. Hydrophobic-motif phosphorylation is not assigned as a direct mTORC2 reaction.
mTORC2-dependent priming supports maturation of this PKC isoform. Hydrophobic-motif phosphorylation is not assigned as a direct mTORC2 reaction.
mTORC2 phosphorylates the turn and hydrophobic motifs of the novel isoform PKCδ, supporting its stability and migration signalling.
edges.notes: Specific residue numbers not asserted. Bibliographic details given External reference not independently verified.

edges.mechanism: PKCε is among the novel PKC isoforms whose mTORC2-dependent priming-site phosphorylation is required for maturation and stability.
edges.notes: Isoform-level data are thinner than for PKCα; residues not asserted.

edges.mechanism: mTORC2 phosphorylates the turn motif of the atypical isoform PKCζ, regulating its stability and activity.
edges.notes: Residue number not asserted. Bibliographic details given External reference not independently verified.

edges.mechanism: mTORC2 phosphorylates the SGK1 hydrophobic motif, which is required for SGK1 activity.

Hepatic mTORC2 supports lipogenesis through SREBP1c and glycolysis through glucokinase; the effect on SREBP1c is relayed by AKT and no direct action of the complex on the transcription factor has been shown.

Hepatic mTORC2 phosphorylates AKT at Ser473, and AKT-dependent glucokinase induction and SREBP1c processing drive lipogenesis; SREBP1 is therefore an indirect output of this complex, and the same transcription factor is driven by both complexes in liver.

Rictor-mTORC2 is required for Th2 differentiation, whereas Rheb-mTORC1 is required for Th1 and Th17; both complexes are additionally required for the glycolytic and glutaminolytic reprogramming of effector activation.
Conditional Rictor deletion in the postnatal forebrain lowers Tiam1 levels and Tiam1-dependent Rac1 activation; the step between the complex and Tiam1 is undefined.
edges.notes: Tiam1 is not a known substrate of the complex, and the relationship rests on a single line of work in one tissue.

edges.mechanism: Forebrain mTORC2 promotes Rac1 activation through Tiam1 and the resulting actin polymerisation in dendritic spines, rather than acting through translational control; conditional Rictor deletion in postnatal forebrain selectively impairs late-phase LTP and long-term memory while sparing early-phase LTP and short-term memory.
edges.notes: The structural, actin-dependent arm of this division of labour has been demonstrated chiefly by one laboratory, in mice and flies.

edges.mechanism: Adipocyte Rictor deletion reduces insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, alters lipid handling and negatively controls whole-body growth.
Adipocyte Rictor deletion alters lipid handling and whole-body growth; as in liver the complexes diverge, so net metabolic effect depends on drug selectivity and exposure.
β-cell Rictor deletion causes mild hyperglycaemia with reduced β-cell mass, decreased AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, nuclear FOXO1 accumulation and elevated p27.

Conditional deletion of Rictor in the postnatal murine forebrain reduces mTORC2 activity and selectively impairs late-phase long-term potentiation and long-term memory while sparing early-phase potentiation and short-term memory; the mechanism is Tiam1–Rac1-dependent actin polymerisation with reduced dendritic spine density, and raising mTORC2 activity pharmacologically enhances long-term memory and reverses its age-associated decline.
edges.notes: The rodent genetics are well supported; the inference that this creates a cognitive deficit missed by standard metabolic monitoring, and its extrapolation to chronic low-dose human dosing, are not.

edges.mechanism: Cardiomyocyte mTORC2 limits apoptosis and tissue loss after ischaemic injury through AKT-dependent anti-apoptotic signalling, complementing the mTORC1 contribution to physiological growth, so agents that ablate both complexes are predicted to be more cardiotoxic than mTORC1-selective ones.
edges.notes: Shown in a myocardial infarction model in which suppression of mTORC2 increased cardiomyocyte apoptosis and tissue damage.

edges.mechanism: mTORC2-dependent SGK1 activity governs ion handling in the distal nephron and therefore sodium balance and blood pressure; renal mTORC2 loss causes salt wasting and hypotension.
Hepatic mTORC2 restrains gluconeogenesis and supports glycolysis and lipogenesis; liver-specific Rictor deletion gives a type-2-diabetes-like phenotype.
Liver-specific Rictor deletion produces glucose intolerance and a phenotype reminiscent of type 2 diabetes, so hepatic mTORC2 is required for normal glucose handling.
mTORC2 contributes to oligodendrocyte differentiation but is not rate-limiting while mTORC1 is intact; the deficit becomes apparent only in the raptor/rictor double mutant.
Rictor loss has modest, largely transient effects; only the double mutant impairs differentiation, so mTORC2 contributes but is not rate-limiting while mTORC1 is intact.

Muscle-specific Rictor deletion is close to phenotypically silent, in contrast to Raptor deletion, which causes dystrophy; the residual mTORC2 contribution is limited to loss of AKT Ser473 phosphorylation and a modest fall in insulin-stimulated glucose uptake.
edges.notes: Negative result, retained because the asymmetry between the complexes in muscle is what predicts the tissue's drug response.

edges.mechanism: mTORC2 supports Th2 effector differentiation and AKT-dependent survival in T lymphocytes; with mTORC1 it governs the metabolic reprogramming of effector activation and restrains Treg commitment.

Loss of total mTOR kinase activity abrogates Th1, Th2 and Th17 differentiation and favours Foxp3 induction, which underlies the preferential expansion of regulatory T cells under rapamycin; restraint of regulatory T cell differentiation is best documented for the AKT–mTORC1 arm, while deletion of Rictor alone has smaller and less consistent effects.
edges.notes: Both complexes have been reported to restrain regulatory T cell differentiation, but loss of mTORC2 alone can leave suppressive function intact or even improved. This is the one tissue setting in which the consequence of inhibition is the desired therapeutic effect rather than a toxicity.

edges.mechanism: Hepatic mTORC2 supports glycolysis via AKT and glucokinase; loss produces a phenotype reminiscent of type 2 diabetes.
Liver-specific Rictor deletion reduces glycolysis and lipogenesis; hepatic mTORC2 activates both through AKT, glucokinase and SREBP1c.
Beta-cell Rictor deletion causes mild hyperglycaemia with reduced beta-cell mass, decreased AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, nuclear FOXO1 accumulation and elevated p27.

Cardiomyocyte mTORC2 is cytoprotective in myocardial ischaemia through AKT-dependent anti-apoptotic signalling: loss of Rictor increases cardiomyocyte apoptosis and infarct damage, whereas shifting signalling from mTORC1 towards mTORC2 reduces it.
Beta-cell Rictor deletion causes mild hyperglycaemia, so intact beta-cell mTORC2 restrains it

Loss of both mTOR complexes in CD4 T cells favours Foxp3+ regulatory T cell differentiation; an independent contribution of mTORC2 to this restraint, acting through AKT, is supported but less consistently than the mTORC1 arm.
edges.context: de novo Treg differentiation in vitro; not mature Treg expansion
edges.notes: Differentiation, expansion and suppressive function are distinct endpoints; mature Tregs require mTORC1 for normal function.

edges.mechanism: mTORC2 phosphorylates AKT at Ser473 in activated T lymphocytes, supporting AKT-dependent survival signalling alongside Th2 differentiation.
In the basal state the mSin1 PH domain folds back onto the mTOR kinase domain and suppresses catalysis; this is the autoinhibited resting conformation of mTORC2.
edges.notes: The mSin1 PH domain is not resolved in published mTORC2 cryo-EM maps, so the autoinhibited conformation rests on biochemical and mutational evidence [360].

edges.mechanism: C-terminal PH domain of mSin1, the PIP3-binding and autoinhibitory element.
Protor-1 joins mTORC2 substoichiometrically through Rictor; it is accessory rather than required for assembly.
Protor-1 binds Rictor as a substoichiometric accessory subunit of mTORC2.
Protor-1 was identified as a Rictor-binding protein and enters mTORC2 through that contact rather than through mTOR.
Protor-1 knockout mice show reduced mTORC2-dependent SGK1 activation and NDRG1 phosphorylation in kidney, with AKT signalling preserved.
edges.notes: Protor-1 loss leaves AKT and PKCalpha hydrophobic- and turn-motif phosphorylation intact, so the requirement is restricted to SGK1 and has been shown only in kidney.

edges.mechanism: Protor-1 is required for efficient mTORC2-mediated SGK1 activation, an effect most evident in kidney.
edges.notes: Protor-1/2 are implicated in SGK1 regulation.

edges.mechanism: Protor-2, the PRR5 paralogue, associates substoichiometrically with mTORC2 via Rictor.
Protor-2 binds Rictor as a substoichiometric accessory subunit of mTORC2.

Protor-2 (PRR5L), the paralogue of Protor-1, binds Rictor and thereby associates with mTORC2 without being required for complex integrity or kinase activity; a binding site shared with Protor-1 and strictly exclusive binding of the two paralogues have not been mapped.

Protor-2 acts within mTORC2 to restrain phosphorylation of PKC-delta by the complex; its degradation downstream of G-alpha-12 permits PKC-delta phosphorylation and promotes cell migration, with no evidence of direct binding to the kinase.

4E-BP1 contains an N-terminal RAIP motif (Arg-Ala-Ile-Pro) that, together with the C-terminal TOS motif, is required for efficient mTORC1-dependent multisite phosphorylation; NMR places its contact on Raptor at a site separate from the TOS pocket.
edges.notes: Whether the RAIP motif contacts Raptor directly is disputed: Beugnet et al. 2003 (J Biol Chem 278:40717-40722) found that the RAIP-containing N-terminal fragment of 4E-BP1 does not bind Raptor.

edges.mechanism: NMR shows that the N-terminal RAIP motif of 4E-BP1 binds Raptor at a site separate from the TOS-binding pocket, so that the two motifs tether 4E-BP1 by avidity and orient its phosphoacceptor region toward the kinase site; mutation of either motif abolishes Raptor co-immunoprecipitation of 4E-BP1.
edges.notes: Beugnet et al. 2003 (J Biol Chem 278:40717-40722) found no Raptor binding by the RAIP-containing N-terminal fragment and concluded that RAIP promotes phosphorylation independently of Raptor binding; a direct RAIP-mTOR contact has not been demonstrated.

edges.mechanism: mSin1 contains a Raf-like, atypical Ras-binding domain between its CRIM and PH domains that binds GTP-loaded H-Ras and K-Ras.
The Akt kinase C-lobe engages an N-terminal mooring formed jointly by mSin1 and Rictor, completing the distal docking surface that selects the substrate.
edges.notes: Supported by a single structural study using semisynthetic trapping probes [597]; not yet independently reproduced.

edges.mechanism: The AKT C-lobe engages an N-terminal mooring formed jointly by mSin1 and Rictor, completing the bipartite docking that positions Ser473 at the active site.
edges.notes: A docking surface remote from the catalytic cleft is in principle a druggable site for genuinely mTORC2-selective inhibitors, which do not presently exist. Rests on the single 2025 structural study [597].

edges.mechanism: In the assembled mTORC2 cryo-EM structures Rictor packs against the FRB bundle, sterically denying access to the FKBP12-rapamycin complex.
Rictor packs against the FRB domain, occluding the FKBP12–rapamycin binding surface; this is the structural basis for rapamycin insensitivity of preassembled mTORC2.
Cryo-EM shows Rictor, together with mSin1, covering the FRB surface of mTOR within mTORC2, which is the structural basis for the rapamycin insensitivity of preassembled mTORC2.
edges.notes: mSin1 (MAPKAP1) contributes to the same occlusion

edges.mechanism: Rictor binds the mTOR N-HEAT solenoid and is required for mTORC2 assembly and integrity; with mSin1 it occludes the FRB domain and forms the N-terminal mooring that docks the AKT C-lobe, whereas the mSin1 CRIM domain provides the principal substrate-docking surface.
Rictor is the defining stoichiometric subunit of mTORC2, binding the mTOR solenoid and bridging to mSin1.
Rictor is the defining subunit that distinguishes mTORC2 from mTORC1 and is raptor-independent.

Rictor, with mSin1, occupies a surface on the mTOR N-HEAT solenoid that overlaps the Raptor footprint, so Raptor and Rictor binding to mTOR are mutually exclusive and the two complexes partition a common mTOR pool.
PRAS40 carries a bona fide TOS motif read by the same Raptor pocket as substrate TOS motifs, which is why it behaves as a competitive rather than allosteric inhibitor.

Raptor binds the C-terminal TOS motif of 4E-BP1 and, according to NMR data, the N-terminal RAIP motif at a separate site, tethering 4E-BP1 so that its phosphoacceptor region is presented to the mTOR active site.
edges.notes: A direct RAIP-Raptor contact is disputed: Beugnet et al. 2003 (J Biol Chem 278:40717-40722) found no Raptor binding by the RAIP-containing N-terminal fragment of 4E-BP1.

edges.mechanism: HIF-1alpha carries a TOS motif recognised by Raptor, coupling mTORC1 directly to hypoxia-responsive transcription.
edges.notes: The HIF-1alpha TOS motif and its Raptor binding were characterised by a single laboratory (Land and Tee 2007).

edges.mechanism: HIF-1alpha carries a TOS motif recognised by the Raptor substrate pocket, the same surface that reads the S6K1, 4E-BP1 and PRAS40 motifs; Raptor binding through this motif is required for mTORC1-dependent HIF-1alpha activity.
edges.notes: The HIF-1alpha TOS motif and its Raptor binding were characterised by a single laboratory (Land and Tee 2007).

edges.mechanism: Raptor wraps the N-HEAT solenoid and projects a substrate-recognition surface outward; because the mTOR cleft is deep and partially occluded, recruitment by Raptor is obligatory, not incidental.
Raptor is the defining stoichiometric subunit of mTORC1, two copies per dimer, wrapped around the N-HEAT solenoid of each mTOR protomer.
Raptor recognises the S6K1 TOR signalling motif, consensus Phe-Asp/Glu-Phi-Asp/Glu-Phi, and this binding is required for mTORC1 to phosphorylate the kinase.
Raptor binds ULK1 in a nutrient-dependent manner, incorporating mTORC1 into the ULK1-ATG13-FIP200 complex and presenting ULK1 for inhibitory phosphorylation at Ser758 (Ser757 in mouse).
edges.notes: manual override: Raptor binds the ULK1 TOS motif to present ULK1 for inhibitory Ser757 phosphorylation by mTORC1; the net effect of the Raptor-ULK1 interaction on ULK1 activity is inhibitory, so a positive sign would mislead sign-aware path queries.

edges.mechanism: Raptor mediates the nutrient-dependent association of mTORC1 with the ULK1-ATG13-FIP200 complex, presenting ULK1 for inhibitory phosphorylation at Ser758 (Ser757 in mouse), which prevents its activation by AMPK; the net effect of the interaction on ULK1 is inhibitory.
edges.notes: manual override: Raptor binds the ULK1 TOS motif to present ULK1 for inhibitory Ser757 phosphorylation by mTORC1; the net effect of the Raptor-ULK1 interaction on ULK1 activity is inhibitory, so a positive sign would mislead sign-aware path queries.

edges.mechanism: LARP1 co-purifies with Raptor/mTORC1; the interaction positions LARP1 for mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation and is sensitive to mTORC1 activity.

PRAS40 carries its own TOS motif (FVMDE, Phe129), which is required for Raptor binding and lets PRAS40 occupy the Raptor substrate-docking site in competition with S6K1 and 4E-BP1. PRAS40 is also itself an mTORC1 substrate at Ser183.
4E-BP1 carries a C-terminal TOS motif (FEMDI) required for Raptor binding and for efficient multisite phosphorylation by mTORC1.
HIF-1alpha is reported to carry an N-terminal TOS motif (Phe99) through which it binds Raptor. Mutating this motif impairs hypoxic HIF activity and p300/CBP binding.
edges.notes: The HIF-1alpha TOS motif has been studied by one research group only, and mTORC1 also raises HIF-1alpha through 4E-BP1- and S6K1-dependent translation.

edges.mechanism: S6K1 carries an N-terminal TOS motif (FDIDL) that is necessary for Raptor binding and for Thr389 phosphorylation.

Raptor recognises the five-residue TOS motif of its clients; point mutation of the motif's phenylalanine abolishes binding to Raptor and mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation, which is the molecular basis of substrate selection by mTORC1.
TRPML1 releases lysosomal Ca2+ into a local microdomain on mTORC1 inhibition or lysosomal stress
TRPML1 is a channel resident in the lysosomal membrane, placing the Ca2+-calcineurin-TFEB step on the lysosomal surface
mSin1 splice isoforms assemble distinct mTORC2 species; the isoform lacking the C-terminal PH domain yields a complex not gated by PIP3.
edges.notes: Alternative splicing of mSin1 generates three mTORC2 species; the assignment comes from a single biochemical study and has not been independently reproduced, although the behaviour of the complex built on the isoform lacking the C-terminal PH domain is consistent with later work showing that the PH domain autoinhibits the complex until PIP3 binds.

edges.mechanism: Activating MTOR mutations are increasingly recognised in renal cell carcinoma, clustering in FAT and kinase domains.
Cancer-associated FAT-domain MTOR substitutions can increase mTOR signalling; the magnitude and substrate profile vary among variants.
edges.context: cancer-associated variants; biochemical and cell models

edges.mechanism: Activating MTOR variants act on the kinase itself and so belong to the proximal-brake class.
Activating MTOR mutations occur in renal cell carcinoma; domain assignment and functional activation must be established for each variant.

Activating kinase-domain MTOR substitutions are recognised in urothelial carcinoma; a patient with a complete response to everolimus plus pazopanib carried two concurrent activating variants, E2014K and E2419K, shown to be activating in vitro.
edges.notes: The response occurred during combined everolimus and pazopanib treatment.

edges.mechanism: Selected MTOR kinase-domain substitutions increase signalling. E2419K was functionally activating in a urothelial cancer exceptional responder; F2108L is an FRB resistance mutation, not a kinase-domain activating substitution.
edges.context: somatic, renal cell and urothelial carcinoma

edges.mechanism: Activating MTOR variants in both the FAT and kinase domains belong to the proximal-brake class and are somatic.
SCF-betaTrCP binds the phosphorylated DEPTOR degron and polyubiquitinates it, committing the inhibitory subunit to proteasomal degradation.

Growth-factor-induced phosphorylation of the DEPTOR degron, primed by mTOR (or by S6K1 and RSK1) and completed by casein kinase 1 alpha, creates a betaTrCP binding site; SCF-betaTrCP then ubiquitinates DEPTOR and targets it for proteasomal degradation, so active mTOR removes its own inhibitor.
beta-TrCP1 is the F-box substrate-receptor subunit of the SCF ligase that destroys DEPTOR.
SCF-betaTrCP recognises the phospho-Ser67 degron of PDCD4 and ubiquitinates it for proteasomal degradation after growth-factor stimulation.

Hypophosphorylated 4E-BP1 binds the dorsal surface of eIF4E through the canonical YXXXXLΦ motif shared with eIF4G and through a secondary site, sequestering eIF4E from eIF4F. Multisite phosphorylation releases eIF4E; in the paralogue 4E-BP2, phosphorylation of Thr37 and Thr46 folds the protein into a β-domain that buries this motif.
4E-BP1 and eIF4G share the eIF4E-binding motif, so 4E-BP1 binding to eIF4E is mutually exclusive with eIF4G and blocks eIF4F assembly on the cap.
4E-BPs mediate mTORC1 control of proliferation but not cell size: 4E-BP1/2-null cells are resistant to the antiproliferative effect of mTORC1 inhibition.
Ribosome profiling attributes TOP mRNA sensitivity to mTORC1 largely to 4E-BPs, whereas LARP1 studies show 4E-BP-independent repression; both arms likely contribute.
edges.notes: Relative contribution of 4E-BP versus LARP1 to TOP repression remains debated.

edges.mechanism: Hypophosphorylated 4E-BP1 sequesters eIF4E and suppresses translation of the structured-5'UTR HIF1A mRNA; mTORC1 phosphorylation relieves this
4E-BPs restrain translation of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs including TFAM and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins; mTORC1 phosphorylation relieves this

Hypophosphorylated 4E-BP1 binds eIF4E and restrains cap-dependent translation of MYC mRNA, whose structured 5′ untranslated region makes it highly dependent on eIF4F; mTORC1 phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 releases eIF4E and raises c-Myc protein.
4E-BP restrains translation of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs including TFAM and respiratory chain components; mTORC1-dependent 4E-BP phosphorylation relieves this.
edges.notes: The primary evidence is translational profiling showing that mTOR inhibition lowers synthesis of TFAM and other nucleus-encoded mitochondrial proteins in wild-type cells but not in cells lacking 4E-BP1 and 4E-BP2.

edges.mechanism: Hypophosphorylated 4E-BP1 sequesters eIF4E and suppresses translation of VEGFA mRNA, which has a long structured 5′ untranslated region; mTORC1 phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 relieves this, adding a translational arm to HIF-1alpha-dependent VEGFA transcription.
4E-BP1 restrains entrainment: Eif4ebp1-null mice show accelerated re-entrainment to a shifted light schedule and larger photic phase shifts, mirroring their elevated VIP levels
edges.notes: Accelerated re-entrainment and larger light-induced phase shifts in 4E-BP1-null mice come from a single genetic study and have not been independently replicated.

edges.mechanism: 4E-BP1 represses translation of Vip mRNA in SCN neurons; 4E-BP1 loss raises VIP levels, accelerating re-entrainment and increasing network synchrony.
edges.notes: PMID 23972597 (Cao R et al., Neuron 2013;79(4):712-724). Repression of VIP translation is supported by the Eif4ebp1-null phenotype in that paper.

edges.mechanism: 4E-BP2, the predominant brain 4E-BP, restrains eIF4F formation; its loss enhances LTP, impairs memory and produces autism-like behaviour via excess eIF4E-dependent translation.

4E-BP2 represses cap-dependent translation at the synapse: in its absence a single train that normally yields only early-phase potentiation induces late-phase LTP, so the induction threshold falls, yet late-phase LTP elicited by repeated high-frequency trains is impaired and hippocampus-dependent memory is deficient. Both excessive and deficient translational signalling are deleterious in brain.
edges.notes: The lowered threshold for late-phase LTP in 4E-BP2-null hippocampus coexists with impaired late-phase LTP after strong stimulation and with deficient hippocampus-dependent memory.

edges.mechanism: Loss of the translational repressor 4E-BP2 produces autism-like behaviour with an increased excitation-to-inhibition ratio, the upper arm of the neuronal requirement for calibrated translational signalling; the accompanying synaptic phenotype is a lowered threshold for late-phase LTP rather than uniformly enhanced potentiation.

The C-terminal DM15 region of LARP1 binds the m7G cap and the adjacent 5'TOP pyrimidine tract at the same time. This occludes the cap from eIF4E and excludes eIF4F from TOP mRNAs when mTORC1 is inactive.
Cap occupancy by LARP1 sterically excludes eIF4E/eIF4F from TOP mRNAs.
LARP1 associates with PABP and poly(A) tails, linking 3' and 5' ends of TOP mRNAs and contributing to their stability and mTORC1-responsive translation.

LARP1 represses TOP mRNAs, which encode the ribosomal proteins and several elongation factors, and so indirectly limits the protein arm of ribosome biogenesis. Relief of this repression on mTORC1 activation lets ribosomal-protein supply scale with the Pol I rRNA and Pol III tRNA and 5S arms.
When mTORC1 is inactive, the LARP1 DM15 domain binds the m7G cap and adjacent 5'TOP motif, repressing translation of ribosomal-protein and elongation-factor mRNAs.
Independently of translational repression, LARP1 (with 40S subunits) protects TOP mRNAs from decay; LARP1 depletion lowers TOP mRNA abundance.
edges.notes: Dual repressor/stabiliser role of LARP1.

edges.mechanism: MAF1 binds the TFIIIB subunit BRF1 and inhibits de novo assembly of TFIIIB-DNA complexes on Pol III promoters, which impairs Pol III recruitment.
edges.notes: Direct Maf1-Brf1 co-immunoprecipitation was shown in yeast. In mammalian cells, MAF1 associates with TFIIIB and Pol III and represses transcription through BRF1 and BRF2.

edges.mechanism: Mammalian MAF1 also represses Pol I transcription, at least partly indirectly, by repressing transcription of TBP, the TATA-binding protein that Pol I initiation complexes require. No direct contact between MAF1 and Pol I has been shown.
Dephosphorylated MAF1 binds the Pol III clamp, rearranging the enzyme to prevent TFIIIB-dependent recruitment and closed-complex formation on tRNA and 5S promoters.
PP2A associates with S6K1 and dephosphorylates it when mTORC1 is inhibited by rapamycin; mTORC1 activity restrains PP2A action on S6K1.
edges.notes: Identity of the physiological S6K1 phosphatase remains debated (PP2A vs PHLPP).

edges.mechanism: PP2A dephosphorylates the activating Ser44 site of TIF-IA/RRN3, reducing Pol I transcription; phosphatase inhibition attenuates rapamycin-induced Ser44 dephosphorylation.
edges.notes: PP2A treatment inactivates TIF-IA in vitro, and calyculin A or okadaic acid prevents rapamycin-induced Ser44 dephosphorylation in cells. Because these inhibitors also act on PP1, PP2A is the most likely cellular phosphatase but not a proven one, and no phosphatase has been identified for Ser199.

edges.mechanism: S6K1 phosphorylates IRS-1 on inhibitory serines, uncoupling it from INSR/PI3K and promoting its degradation — blunting PI3K–AKT output (negative feedback).
edges.notes: Sites are human IRS-1 numbering: Ser307 corresponds to mouse Ser302 and Ser636/Ser639 to rat Ser632/Ser635. Human Ser312 (mouse Ser307) is phosphorylated by JNK and IKK rather than by S6K1. This feedback explains the rebound AKT activation seen on acute mTORC1 inhibition [500].

edges.mechanism: S6K1 phosphorylates IRS-1 on inhibitory serines, promoting its degradation and blunting PI3K-AKT output from the insulin receptor.
edges.notes: Sites are human IRS-1 numbering; the primary reports use the mouse and rat equivalents Ser302 and Ser632/Ser635. Underlies mTORC1-associated insulin resistance and the paradoxical protection from steatosis seen after liver Tsc1 deletion.

edges.mechanism: S6K1, together with RSK1, was reported to phosphorylate the DEPTOR betaTrCP degron (Ser286, Ser287, Ser291) after growth-factor stimulation, promoting SCF-betaTrCP-dependent DEPTOR degradation. Another laboratory found that S6K inhibition or knockdown does not change DEPTOR turnover and attributed degron phosphorylation to mTOR and CK1alpha.
edges.notes: Opposing evidence: Gao et al. 2011, Mol Cell 44:290-303 (PMID 22017875).

edges.mechanism: S6K1 phosphorylates mSin1 at Thr86 and Thr398, impairing mTORC2 complex integrity and suppressing downstream AKT signalling.
edges.notes: Yang et al. 2015 (Cell Rep 12:937-943; PMID 26235620) reported that AKT-mediated phosphorylation of mSin1 Thr86 enhances mTORC2 activity, the opposite sign at the same residue.

edges.mechanism: S6K1-dependent mSin1 Thr86/Thr398 phosphorylation was reported to disrupt mTORC2 and reduce AKT Ser473 phosphorylation.
edges.notes: Liu et al. reported negative regulation involving Thr86/Thr398; Yang et al. reported positive AKT-dependent regulation specifically at Thr86.

edges.mechanism: S6K1 phosphorylates mTOR at Ser2448 in the negative regulatory domain; the site is a convenient activity marker but has no demonstrated effect on catalysis.
edges.notes: Established as a phosphorylation event; its functional consequence for mTOR activity is not established.

edges.mechanism: mTORC1-activated S6K1 directly phosphorylates Rictor at Thr1135, creating a 14-3-3 binding site without altering mTORC2 assembly or in vitro kinase activity. Two studies found that a T1135A mutant raises AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, indicating feedback inhibition, whereas two others saw no major change in mTORC2 activity or AKT phosphorylation.
edges.notes: Boulbès et al. 2010 [53] detected Thr1135 phosphorylation in mTORC2-deficient cells, suggesting that it may also regulate functions of Rictor outside mTORC2.

edges.mechanism: mTORC1-activated S6K1 directly phosphorylates Rictor at Thr1135, creating a 14-3-3 binding site without altering mTORC2 assembly or in vitro kinase activity. Two studies found that a T1135A mutant raises AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, indicating feedback inhibition, whereas two others saw no major change in mTORC2 activity or AKT phosphorylation.
edges.notes: Boulbès et al. 2010 [53] detected Thr1135 phosphorylation in mTORC2-deficient cells, suggesting that it may also regulate functions of Rictor outside mTORC2.

edges.mechanism: mTORC1-activated S6K1 directly phosphorylates Rictor at Thr1135, creating a 14-3-3 binding site without altering mTORC2 assembly or in vitro kinase activity. Two studies found that a T1135A mutant raises AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, indicating feedback inhibition, whereas two others saw no major change in mTORC2 activity or AKT phosphorylation.
edges.notes: Boulbès et al. 2010 [53] detected Thr1135 phosphorylation in mTORC2-deficient cells, suggesting that it may also regulate functions of Rictor outside mTORC2.

edges.mechanism: S6K1 deletion yields small mice and cells; S6Ks control cell size (growth) whereas 4E-BPs control proliferation downstream of mTORC1.
S6K1 phosphorylates eEF2 kinase at Ser366, reducing its activity at physiological Ca2+ and thereby lowering eEF2 Thr56 phosphorylation and accelerating elongation.
S6K1 phosphorylates eIF4B at Ser422 in a rapamycin-sensitive manner, enhancing eIF4B recruitment to the preinitiation complex and eIF4A helicase stimulation on structured 5'UTRs.

S6K1 phosphorylates CBP80, the large subunit of the nuclear cap-binding complex, at residues that are also phosphorylated in cells in a growth-factor-dependent, rapamycin-sensitive manner, and S6K1 is found together with SKAR on CBP80-bound spliced mRNAs.
edges.notes: The phosphorylated residues of CBP80 have not been mapped, and the consequence for cap binding and splicing remains undetermined.

edges.mechanism: S6K1 phosphorylates PDCD4 at Ser67, creating a phosphodegron for betaTrCP-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, relieving eIF4A inhibition.

Phosphorylation of the S6K1 hydrophobic motif at Thr389 by mTORC1 creates a docking site for the PIF pocket of PDK1, which then phosphorylates the S6K1 activation loop at Thr229. The mTORC1 and PDK1 inputs to S6K1 are therefore sequential rather than independent.
edges.notes: Thr389 lies in the hydrophobic motif of S6K1, the docking partner; PDK1 itself is not phosphorylated in this interaction.

edges.mechanism: S6K activity controls a ribosome-biogenesis transcriptional programme (rRNA processing factors, Pol I/III cofactors) in addition to rDNA transcription.
edges.notes: The mammalian evidence comes mainly from liver and cells lacking both S6K1 and S6K2, in which the feeding-induced ribosome-biogenesis transcriptional programme fails. The requirement for S6K1 in UBF-dependent rDNA transcription is a separate and better-supported arm.

edges.mechanism: Active S6K1 phosphorylates 40S ribosomal protein S6 in ordered fashion (Ser236 first); phosphorylation influences cell size and glucose homeostasis.
edges.notes: Ser247 is phosphorylated by CK1 after priming.

edges.mechanism: The C-terminal autoinhibitory pseudosubstrate domain restrains S6K1; proline-directed phosphorylation (Ser411/Thr421/Ser424) relieves it, allowing Thr389/Thr229 phosphorylation.

S6K1, but not S6K2, binds SKAR and phosphorylates it at Ser383 and Ser385 in response to insulin and other mitogens, in a rapamycin-sensitive manner. Depletion of SKAR reduces cell size, but the functional consequence of these two phosphorylations has not been determined.

S6K1 activity is required for mTOR-dependent phosphorylation of the UBF carboxy-terminal activation domain, which enhances UBF binding to SL1 and Pol I transcription of rDNA. Rapamycin causes rapid dephosphorylation of this domain, and a constitutively active, rapamycin-resistant S6K1 reverses it. Direct phosphorylation of UBF by S6K1 has not been shown, so the relationship is S6K1-dependent rather than a proven kinase-substrate interaction.
edges.notes: Rapamycin-sensitive; whether S6K1 phosphorylates UBF directly or via an intermediate kinase is not fully resolved.

edges.mechanism: S6K1 phosphorylates CAD at Ser1859, promoting its oligomerisation and raising flux through the first three steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis
edges.notes: Demonstrated independently by two groups in the same year, one by unbiased phosphoproteomics.

edges.mechanism: S6K1 is required for insulin-stimulated proteolytic processing of SREBP-1c, providing an S6K1-dependent limb of mTORC1 lipogenic output
S6K1 phosphorylates BMAL1, licensing its association with the translational machinery and so coupling nutrient status and mTORC1 activity to rhythmic cap-dependent translation.
edges.notes: Site numbering is mouse BMAL1 (Ser42) as reported by Lipton 2015; confirm residue numbering against the human sequence before display.

edges.mechanism: Chronic mTORC1 activation in obesity contributes to insulin resistance through S6K1-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation of IRS-1, and through lipotoxic consequences of constrained storage capacity.
Germline deletion of S6K1 extends median lifespan by about 19% in female mice, with no significant effect in males, placing one mTORC1 substrate arm within the longevity mechanism.
edges.notes: The lifespan effect comes from a single mouse cohort and has not been independently replicated; S6K1-null females also showed increased AMPK activation and a caloric restriction-like gene expression profile.

edges.mechanism: S6K2 phosphorylates rpS6 redundantly with S6K1 and is the principal rpS6 kinase in S6K1-null cells; residual Ser235/236 in double knockouts derives from RSK.
TIF-IA binds initiation-competent Pol I and bridges it to the SL1 promoter-selectivity factor at the rDNA promoter.

RRN3/TIF-IA binds both Pol I and the TAF1B subunit of promoter-bound SL1/TIF-IB, bridging initiation-competent polymerase to the rDNA promoter. This bridging step is the point at which the mTORC1 input on TIF-IA Ser44 is converted into pre-initiation complex formation.
UBF binds the rDNA promoter and enhancer, recruits SL1 and stabilises Pol I preinitiation complexes; its activity is mTOR/S6K1-dependent.

AMBRA1 binds Beclin-1 and promotes the activity of the autophagy-specific class III PI3K complex I; it is a regulatory partner of the complex rather than one of its core subunits, which are VPS34, VPS15, Beclin-1 and ATG14L.
Released AMBRA1 recruits TRAF6 to catalyse K63-linked ULK1 ubiquitylation, promoting ULK1 self-association, stability and activity
edges.notes: External reference not independently verified.

edges.mechanism: ATG101 binds ATG13 through HORMA-domain interaction, stabilising it within the initiation complex
ATG13 bridges ULK1 and FIP200 and is required for complex integrity and ULK1 activity
ATG14L is the subunit that targets the VPS34 complex to the autophagy initiation site, defining complex I
p300-mediated acetylation of ATG proteins (ATG5, ATG7, ATG12, LC3) suppresses autophagosome formation; p300 depletion induces autophagy
edges.notes: External reference not independently verified.

edges.mechanism: p300 acetylates lipogenic regulators to promote de novo lipid synthesis, providing an acetylation-dependent limb of mTORC1 lipid output
edges.notes: External reference not independently verified.

edges.mechanism: Grb10 binds and desensitises the IGF-1 receptor in the same manner as INSR.
Grb10 binds and desensitises the IGF-1 receptor, extending the feedback brake to IGF-1 signalling
Stabilised Grb10 binds the activated insulin receptor kinase (SH2/BPS domains), desensitising receptor signalling to IRS/PI3K.
Stabilised Grb10 binds the insulin receptor and desensitises downstream signalling, independently of the S6K1-IRS-1 arm

When mTORC1 is inactive, dephosphorylated lipin 1 enters the nucleus and lowers nuclear SREBP protein abundance, SREBP promoter activity and SREBP target-gene expression; mTORC1 phosphorylation keeps lipin 1 cytoplasmic and relieves this inhibition. Direct binding or sequestration of SREBP by lipin 1 has not been shown.
Calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB, releasing 14-3-3 and permitting nuclear entry and CLEAR-network transcription
edges.notes: Pharmacologically relevant: calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine) would be expected to oppose this step.

edges.mechanism: FIP200 is the scaffold subunit of the ULK1 initiation complex and is required for ULK1 stability and phagophore nucleation
Pacer (RUBCNL) promotes autophagosome maturation by engaging STX17 and the HOPS tethering complex and by relieving Rubicon-mediated inhibition of VPS34.
TFE3 binds the same CLEAR elements as TFEB and drives lysosomal and autophagy gene expression, providing partial redundancy
edges.notes: TFE3 is itself subject to mTORC1-dependent cytoplasmic retention. Its binding to CLEAR elements and induction of lysosomal and autophagy genes was shown by Martina et al. (Sci Signal 2014).

edges.mechanism: Nuclear TFEB binds CLEAR E-box elements and drives approximately 470 lysosomal and autophagy genes coordinately
MCOLN1 is itself a CLEAR target gene, so TFEB activation raises TRPML1 expression and amplifies the Ca2+-calcineurin input back onto TFEB
edges.notes: TRPML1-dependent calcineurin activation acts upstream of TFEB. Medina et al. (2015) describe MCOLN1 as a direct TFEB target, forming a positive feedback loop.

edges.mechanism: TFEB drives RRAGD expression, increasing Rag-dependent lysosomal recruitment of mTORC1 - a transcriptional feed-forward loop onto mTORC1
edges.context: renal and pancreatic tumours with MiT/TFE activation
edges.notes: Explains how MiT/TFE activation can drive mTORC1 rather than only responding to it.

edges.mechanism: TFEB and TFE3, the mTORC1-controlled transcription factors of the autophagy–lysosome programme, feed back onto peripheral clock gene expression, coupling catabolic state to the clock.
edges.notes: A single-laboratory finding, hence the emerging grading.

edges.mechanism: ULK1 phosphorylates all three AMPK subunits (several Ser/Thr sites on alpha1, beta2, gamma1), reducing AMPK activity: a negative feedback loop terminating the autophagy-inducing signal.
edges.notes: Single primary study with limited independent replication.

edges.mechanism: ULK1 phosphorylates Raptor strongly at Ser855 and Ser859 and moderately at Ser792, which hinders 4E-BP1 docking on Raptor and lowers mTORC1 output toward S6K1 and 4E-BP1.
edges.notes: The rise in Raptor Ser863 phosphorylation after ULK1 overexpression is mTORC1-dependent, so Ser863 is not a direct ULK1 site.

edges.mechanism: Activated ULK1 phosphorylates its complex partner ATG13 at several sites within the initiation complex; the modification accompanies autophagy induction and promotes ATG13 recruitment to damaged mitochondria during mitophagy, but it is not known to activate ATG13 itself.
ULK1 phosphorylates ATG14L at Ser29, stimulating VPS34 activity in the autophagy-specific complex and opposing the inhibitory mTORC1 marks
edges.notes: External reference not independently verified.

edges.mechanism: ULK1/Atg1 phosphorylates ATG9 to control its trafficking to and from the phagophore assembly site, a required step for membrane delivery during autophagosome formation.
edges.context: demonstrated for Atg1–Atg9 in yeast; the mammalian ULK1–ATG9A equivalent is supported but less firmly established
edges.notes: Do not upgrade without a mammalian reference.

edges.mechanism: ULK1 kinase activity initiates phagophore formation; it is the principal node through which nutrient and energy status gate autophagy
ULK1 phosphorylates Beclin-1 at Ser14, activating VPS34 lipid-kinase activity within autophagy-specific class III PI3K complexes

Active ULK1 phosphorylates FIP200 within the initiation complex; the modification accompanies autophagy induction, although a specific requirement for it in phagophore nucleation has not been demonstrated.
UVRAG defines VPS34 complex II, mutually exclusive with ATG14L.
WIPI2 binds ATG16L1 directly and recruits the ATG12–ATG5–ATG16L1 conjugation machinery to PI3P-positive phagophores, licensing LC3 lipidation.
XPLN binds Rictor and suppresses mTORC2-mediated AKT Ser473 phosphorylation independently of its Rho GEF activity.
edges.notes: Single-group finding with limited replication.

edges.mechanism: Loss of mTORC2-primed PKC protein produces cytoskeletal defects, the mechanistic link between mTORC2 and actin organisation.
PKC-dependent Rho-family signalling supports adhesion dynamics, which fail when mTORC2 priming is lost.
Reduced PKC protein in mTORC2-deficient cells impairs migration.
mTORC2-dependent PKC activity is required for epithelial apicobasal polarity; mTORC2-deficient cells show polarity defects.

Loss of mTORC2 lowers PKC protein and activity and reduces Rho-family signalling, of which Rac1 is a member; a direct action of PKC on Rac1, plausibly through Rac guanine-nucleotide exchange factors, has not been established, and Rac1 has also been reported to act upstream of mTOR.
edges.notes: Inferred from the cytoskeletal phenotype of mTORC2-deficient cells rather than from a defined molecular step.

edges.mechanism: mTORC2-deficient cells lose PKC protein and show Rho-pathway and actomyosin defects; the connection from PKC to RhoA is inferred from this phenotype rather than demonstrated as a direct activating step.
edges.notes: Inferred from the cytoskeletal phenotype of mTORC2-deficient cells rather than from a defined molecular step.

edges.mechanism: Atypical PKC activity within the Par3–Par6–aPKC module specifies the apical domain by phosphorylating Par3, Lgl and Par1; PKC-iota/lambda and PKC-zeta act redundantly in mammalian epithelia, and their mTORC2-dependent stability links the complex to polarity.
edges.notes: PKC-iota/lambda is the predominant atypical PKC in mammalian epithelia and acts redundantly with PKC-zeta.

edges.mechanism: SGK1 signalling increases Na+/K+-ATPase activity and surface abundance, maintaining the basolateral gradient for transepithelial sodium transport; the alpha1 subunit has not been shown to be a direct substrate of the kinase.

Coexpression of SGK1 increases CLC-K/barttin chloride channel activity in heterologous systems, which would complete the transcellular salt transport route; phosphorylation of the channel or of barttin has not been demonstrated.

SGK1 phosphorylates FOXO3a at Thr32 and Ser315, promoting 14-3-3 binding and nuclear exclusion. SGK1 and AKT phosphorylate overlapping but non-identical sites, so SGK1 provides a parallel, AKT-independent route from mTORC2 to FOXO suppression.
edges.notes: The SGK1 arm matters because it is the reason SGK1 inhibition is not functionally redundant with AKT inhibition.

edges.mechanism: SGK1 phosphorylates NDRG1, the standard cellular readout of mTORC2–SGK1 pathway activity.
edges.notes: Bibliographic details given External reference not independently verified.

edges.mechanism: SGK1 phosphorylates Nedd4-2, creating 14-3-3 binding sites that prevent it from ubiquitinating ENaC.
edges.notes: Residue numbers not asserted. Bibliographic details given External reference not independently verified.

edges.mechanism: SGK1 raises ENaC surface expression and open probability chiefly indirectly, by phosphorylating Nedd4-2 and relieving ubiquitin-dependent channel retrieval; direct phosphorylation of the channel alpha subunit has been reported in heterologous expression systems and may contribute to the rise in open probability.
SGK1 phosphorylates TSC2 at a site overlapping the AKT site, relieving TSC complex GAP activity toward Rheb and sustaining mTORC1 activity independently of AKT.

SGK1 stimulates sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron, chiefly by phosphorylating NEDD4-2 and so stabilising the epithelial sodium channel at the apical membrane, and it additionally supports Na+/K+-ATPase and CLC-K-dependent transport, with consequences for blood pressure.
A minor subset of mTORC2 associates with ribosomes; the association is PI3K- and growth-factor-responsive and constitutes an activating input to the complex.
A minor subset of mTORC2 associates with ribosomes; this association activates the complex and provides a growth-factor-responsive input.
Ribosome abundance sets translational capacity; mTORC1-driven ribosome biogenesis is therefore a prerequisite for sustained anabolic protein synthesis.
TFIIIB (Brf1-containing) recruits Pol III to TFIIIC-bound tRNA and 5S genes and is the main target of growth-regulated Pol III control.
Cyclin D1 partners CDK4/6 to phosphorylate RB and drive the G1/S transition, linking eIF4F-dependent cyclin D1 translation to cell-cycle entry.
eEF2 catalyses GTP-dependent ribosomal translocation; relief of eEF2K by S6K1 therefore increases elongation rate.
eEF2K phosphorylates eEF2 at Thr56 in the GTP-binding domain, preventing eEF2 from binding the ribosome and halting translocation.
Inactive S6K1 is bound to eIF3; Thr389 phosphorylation by eIF3-recruited mTORC1 releases S6K1 to phosphorylate rpS6 and eIF4B at the preinitiation complex.
eIF4A is the DEAD-box helicase subunit of eIF4F that unwinds 5'UTR secondary structure for 43S scanning.
Ser422-phosphorylated eIF4B shows increased association with eIF3, integrating it into the 43S preinitiation complex.
eIF4B is a cofactor that stimulates eIF4A ATPase and RNA-helicase activity, promoting unwinding of structured 5' untranslated regions during scanning.

eIF4B stimulates eIF4A helicase activity on structured 5'UTRs. Its depletion selectively reduces translation of c-Myc mRNA, together with other structured-5'UTR mRNAs such as Cdc25C, ODC, Bcl-2 and XIAP.
edges.notes: S6K1-eIF4B-dependent control of c-Myc translation and glutamine metabolism was reported in a study that has since been retracted (Csibi et al. 2014, Curr Biol).

edges.mechanism: Binding to eIF4E protects hypophosphorylated 4E-BP1 from ubiquitination by the KLHL25-CUL3 ligase. When eIF4E is depleted, hypophosphorylated 4E-BP1 is degraded while hyperphosphorylated 4E-BP1 is spared, so 4E-BP1 levels track eIF4E abundance.
eIF4E binds the m7G cap and nucleates eIF4F assembly by recruiting eIF4G.

eIF4E recruits the eIF4G scaffold through the canonical YXXXXLΦ eIF4E-binding motif, nucleating eIF4F assembly on the cap. The 4E-BPs carry the same motif and engage the same dorsal surface of eIF4E, so their binding excludes eIF4G.

Released eIF4E drives the proliferative translational programme (cyclin D1, c-Myc, Mcl-1); eIF4E overexpression is transforming in vivo and the proliferative output of mTORC1 is specifically 4E-BP/eIF4E-dependent rather than S6K-dependent.
Ser209-phosphorylated eIF4E promotes translation of Per1 mRNA in the SCN, converting a light pulse into a rise in PER protein and hence a phase shift
edges.notes: Rests on a single report of light-regulated, eIF4E phosphorylation-dependent Per1 translation in the suprachiasmatic nucleus; not independently replicated.

edges.mechanism: eIF4E-dependent translational control also governs Per2 protein output in the SCN, coupling translation-initiation state to the negative limb
edges.notes: From a single report showing that eIF4E phosphorylation promotes translation of both Per1 and Per2 mRNAs in the suprachiasmatic nucleus; not independently replicated.

edges.mechanism: Assembled eIF4F recruits the 43S complex to capped mRNAs; its availability is rate-limiting for cap-dependent initiation.
Cyclin D1 mRNA has a structured 5'UTR whose translation is preferentially sensitive to eIF4E availability and 4E-BP status.

Release of eIF4E from the 4E-BPs downstream of mTORC1 increases eIF4F-dependent translation of HIF-1α mRNA. This raises expression of the HIF-1 glycolytic targets GLUT1, hexokinase 2, PFKFB3, PKM2 and LDHA.
mTORC1 promotes survival through 4E-BP/eIF4E-dependent translation of Mcl-1 mRNA.
c-Myc mRNA (structured 5'UTR) is translated in an eIF4F/eIF4A-dependent manner downstream of mTORC1-4E-BP signalling.
VEGF mRNA translation is eIF4E-sensitive, linking the 4E-BP arm to angiogenesis.
eIF4G-eIF3 interaction bridges cap-bound eIF4F to the 43S preinitiation complex; insulin stimulates this association in an mTOR-dependent manner.
eIF4G is the eIF4F scaffold binding eIF4E, eIF4A, eIF3, PABP and MNK.
MNK docks on the C-terminus of eIF4G to phosphorylate eIF4E; 4E-BP sequestration of eIF4E therefore also prevents Ser209 phosphorylation.

TFIIIC bound to the internal promoter recruits TFIIIB (BRF1-TBP-BDP1) to the upstream region, and TFIIIB in turn loads Pol III. tRNA genes use a type 2 A-box/B-box promoter, whereas 5S rRNA genes use a type 1 promoter at which TFIIIC binding also requires TFIIIA.
HIF-1 binds a hypoxia-response element in the BNIP3 promoter, strongly inducing BNIP3 under hypoxia (mitophagy, Rheb binding).
HIF-1 binds hypoxia-response elements in the REDD1/RTP801 (DDIT4) promoter, rapidly inducing REDD1 mRNA and protein under hypoxia.
HIF-1alpha induces hexokinase 2, committing imported glucose to glycolysis as glucose-6-phosphate
HIF-1alpha induces LDHA, regenerating NAD+ and sustaining high glycolytic flux with lactate export
HIF-1alpha induces PFKFB3, raising fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and allosterically activating PFK1
HIF-1alpha raises PKM2 expression; the M2 isoform supports the biosynthetic rather than purely catabolic use of glycolytic carbon
HIF-1alpha binds hypoxia-response elements in the SLC2A1 promoter, raising GLUT1 expression and glucose uptake
HIF-1alpha, with HIF-1beta (ARNT), binds a hypoxia-response element in the VEGFA 5′-flanking region and induces VEGFA transcription.
edges.notes: VEGF-A is also controlled translationally through 4E-BP1–eIF4E, so mTORC1 raises VEGF-A both through HIF-1alpha-driven transcription and through cap-dependent translation.

edges.mechanism: ERK/p38-activated MNK1/2 phosphorylate eIF4E Ser209; dispensable for global translation but promotes tumorigenesis and translation of select mRNAs.
c-Myc binds TFIIIB through BRF1 and is recruited to tRNA and 5S rRNA genes, directly activating Pol III transcription independently of its Pol II target genes.
c-Myc, itself translated in a 4E-BP/eIF4B-dependent manner, transcriptionally induces ribosomal-protein genes, Pol I/III cofactors (UBF, TIF-IA, Brf1) and rRNA processing factors.
c-Myc transcriptionally represses miR-23a and miR-23b, relieving their repression of the glutaminase transcript and raising glutaminase protein, which increases conversion of glutamine to glutamate.
edges.notes: mTORC1-dependent c-Myc translation supports glutamine anaplerosis. The miR-23a/b route to glutaminase was established in human B-cell and prostate cancer cells.

edges.mechanism: Poly(A)-binding protein bound to the 3' poly(A) tail binds the N-terminal region of eIF4G. This circularises the mRNA and stimulates 43S recruitment and cap-dependent initiation.
PDCD4 MA3 domains bind eIF4A, blocking its helicase activity and its interaction with eIF4G, thereby suppressing translation of structured-5'UTR mRNAs.
The tandem MA3 domains of PDCD4 bind eIF4A at the surface that eIF4G uses. PDCD4 therefore both inhibits eIF4A helicase activity and prevents eIF4A from being incorporated into eIF4F through eIF4G.
edges.notes: PDCD4 also binds the middle region of eIF4G (residues 635-1039) and prevents eIF4A from binding the eIF4G C-terminal region (residues 1040-1560).

edges.mechanism: PDCD4 suppresses neoplastic transformation and inhibits eIF4A-dependent translation of mRNAs with structured 5'UTRs. Its S6K1- and βTrCP-dependent degradation after mitogenic stimulation is required for the full rise in protein synthesis and cell growth after mTORC1 activation, so its effect on proliferation is indirect.
Pol I transcribes the rDNA repeats into the 47S pre-rRNA, the rate-limiting step of ribosome biogenesis coordinated by mTORC1.
Pol III transcribes 5S rRNA genes under MAF1/mTORC1 control, supplying the 60S subunit component.
Pol III transcribes tRNA genes; output rises when mTORC1 phosphorylates and inactivates MAF1.
47S pre-rRNA is processed into 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNAs and assembled with ribosomal proteins in the nucleolus into 40S and 60S subunits.
rpS6 phosphorylation is a determinant of cell size: phospho-null rpS6 knock-in mice have smaller cells (notably beta-cells) and impaired glucose homeostasis.
rpS6 (eS6) is a 40S small-subunit ribosomal protein located near the mRNA/tRNA binding site.
5S rRNA is incorporated with RPL5/RPL11 into the 60S large subunit central protuberance.
SKAR (Aly/REF-like) is deposited with the exon junction complex on newly spliced mRNAs.

SKAR recruits activated S6K1 to newly spliced messenger ribonucleoproteins carrying the exon junction complex, which was reported to raise the translation efficiency of spliced relative to unspliced transcripts.
edges.notes: Reported by a single laboratory and not independently reproduced. The model of a distinct cap-binding-complex-dependent pioneer round of translation, on which the proposed mechanism rests, is itself debated.

edges.mechanism: SL1/TIF-IB (TBP plus TAF1A/TAF1B/TAF1C) binds the rDNA core promoter and, together with UBF, nucleates the Pol I pre-initiation complex; no Pol I initiation occurs without it.
TOP mRNAs encode essentially all ribosomal proteins plus eEF1A, eEF2 and PABP; their mTORC1/LARP1-controlled translation scales ribosomal-protein supply with rRNA synthesis.
tRNA supply, scaled with ribosome production via mTORC1-MAF1, is required for elongation capacity.
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 supplies malonyl-CoA, the rate-limiting substrate for fatty acid synthase.

ATF4, induced through eIF2alpha phosphorylation, is necessary and sufficient for transcriptional induction of REDD1 (DDIT4) during ER stress, and together with C/EBP-beta drives REDD1 expression during oxidative stress; REDD1 then suppresses mTORC1 through TSC2.

ATF4 induces SESN2 transcription downstream of GCN2 during amino-acid deprivation and during ER stress; the induced Sestrin2 is required to sustain mTORC1 repression by keeping mTORC1 off the lysosome.
mTORC1-driven ATF4 promotes glutathione synthesis alongside protein synthesis, coupling anabolic signalling to redox buffering
ATF4 induces the mitochondrial folate-cycle enzyme MTHFD2, the step through which mTORC1 couples one-carbon metabolism to purine supply
ATF4 (CREB2) drives SIRT4 transcription; mTORC1 represses SIRT4 indirectly by promoting proteasome-dependent degradation of ATF4.
edges.notes: ATF4 (CREB2)-driven SIRT4 transcription and its loss under high mTORC1 activity have been reported in one study; this contrasts with the mTORC1-dependent translational induction of ATF4 that drives purine and glutathione synthesis.

edges.mechanism: The ATG12–ATG5–ATG16L1 complex acts as the E3-like ligase that conjugates LC3/GABARAP proteins to phagophore phosphatidylethanolamine, a step required for autophagosome expansion and closure.
Beclin-1 is the core coiled-coil subunit of the autophagy-specific class III PI3K complex
Beclin-1 is shared between VPS34 complexes I and II; complex II substitutes UVRAG for ATG14L and functions in autophagosome maturation and endosomal trafficking.
CAD catalyses the committed early steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis, producing dihydroorotate from glutamine and bicarbonate
C/EBPβ binds and activates autophagy gene promoters, generating the daily rhythm of autophagic flux in liver
Fatty acid synthase performs the iterative condensation producing palmitate, the committed output of de novo lipogenesis.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase catalyses the first and rate-limiting oxidative step of the pentose phosphate pathway, reducing NADP+ to NADPH. This is the specific enzymatic step by which the SREBP–G6PD arm supplies reducing equivalents.
G6PD catalyses the rate-limiting oxidative step, supplying NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotides
Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyses the glutamate-to-alpha-ketoglutarate step that makes glutaminolysis an input to lysosomal mTORC1 activation
Glutamate dehydrogenase converts glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate, feeding glutamine carbon into the TCA cycle

During glucose deprivation hexokinase-II, lacking bound glucose-6-phosphate, binds Raptor through a TOS-like motif and inhibits mTORC1, promoting protective autophagy; G6P binding prevents the interaction.
edges.notes: Single primary study; HK2 is itself an mTORC1/HIF-1 output (feedback).

edges.mechanism: Hexokinase 2 converts glucose to glucose-6-phosphate at the entry to glycolysis; glucose-6-phosphate can also feed other pathways.
HMG-CoA reductase catalyses the rate-limiting conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, committing carbon to sterol synthesis.
Cell-surface IL-1alpha signals through IL1R-NF-kB to sustain the pro-inflammatory secretory programme of senescent cells
IL-1alpha acts upstream of the IL1 receptor-NF-kB arm that sustains the SASP transcriptional programme.
LDHA converts pyruvate to lactate with NAD+ regeneration, permitting sustained aerobic glycolytic flux
MTHFD2 drives the mitochondrial tetrahydrofolate cycle, generating formyl units used for nucleotide synthesis
Formyl-tetrahydrofolate produced by the MTHFD2-dependent cycle supplies carbon to the purine ring, demonstrated by metabolic tracing
De novo fatty acid and sterol synthesis consume NADPH as the reductant, which couples the pentose phosphate arm to the lipogenic arm.
NRF1 induces TFAM expression, coupling the nuclear transcriptional programme to mitochondrial DNA replication and transcription.
Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate produced by PFKFB3 allosterically activates PFK1, the principal flux-controlling step
WIPI2 is a PROPPIN-family PI3P effector whose recruitment to the phagophore depends on direct PI3P binding through its beta-propeller.
PI(3)P generated by complex I recruits WIPI proteins and the ATG conjugation machinery, committing the phagophore to elongation
The ATG14L-containing VPS34 complex phosphorylates phosphatidylinositol at the 3-position to generate PI3P on the nascent phagophore.

UVRAG-containing class III PI3K complex II is implicated in late autophagy, with UVRAG engaging the class C Vps/HOPS tethering complex to promote autophagosome fusion with late endosomes and lysosomes. This maturation function is genetically separable from UVRAG binding to Beclin-1, so whether it requires the lipid-kinase activity of complex II is not settled.
PKM2 catalyses the final glycolytic step; its regulated low-activity state diverts upstream intermediates into biosynthesis
PPARgamma is the master transcriptional driver of adipocyte differentiation and lipid-storage gene expression
edges.notes: External reference not independently verified.

edges.mechanism: PGC-1alpha coactivates the nuclear transcriptional programme for mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative metabolism
PGC-1alpha coactivates NRF1 on the promoters of nuclear-encoded respiratory and mitochondrial biogenesis genes.
Ribose-5-phosphate is converted to PRPP, the committed substrate for de novo purine synthesis; links the pentose phosphate arm to the ATF4–MTHFD2 purine arm.

Ribose-5-phosphate is converted to PRPP, which UMP synthase uses to convert orotate to OMP before decarboxylating it to UMP; this step lies downstream of CAD and DHODH and links the pentose phosphate arm to the S6K1–CAD pyrimidine arm.
SIRT4 ADP-ribosylates glutamate dehydrogenase and inhibits it; its repression downstream of mTORC1 releases the enzyme
edges.notes: External reference not independently verified.

edges.mechanism: GLUT1 mediates facilitative glucose import across the plasma membrane, raising intracellular glucose availability
Nuclear SREBP1 induces acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1, catalysing the committed step of de novo lipogenesis.
Nuclear SREBP1 induces fatty acid synthase, one of the lipogenic target genes whose induction defines the mTORC1–SREBP1 arm.
SREBP-dependent induction of G6PD activates the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway downstream of mTORC1
Nuclear SREBP1 induces ACC, FASN and SCD1, driving de novo fatty-acid synthesis
SREBP1c induces the lipogenic gene programme (FASN, ACC, SCD1).
SREBP1c induces the lipogenic enzyme battery; this is the arm through which hepatic mTORC1 contributes to steatosis under hyperinsulinaemic conditions.
Nuclear SREBP1 induces stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1, required for monounsaturated fatty acid supply to membrane lipid and triglyceride synthesis.
Nuclear SREBP2 induces HMGCR, HMGCS1 and LDLR, driving the sterol biosynthetic and uptake programme
