Nuclear SREBP2 induces HMG-CoA reductase and other mevalonate pathway genes; mTOR activity is required for full expression of this sterol biosynthetic programme.
TFAM packages mitochondrial DNA and activates its transcription; its loss abolishes mtDNA maintenance and oxidative phosphorylation, making it a required effector of mitochondrial biogenesis.
pThr246-PRAS40 binds 14-3-3, which displaces PRAS40 from Raptor/mTORC1 and so derepresses substrate access.
edges.notes: Binding requires prior AKT phosphorylation of Thr246; inhibiting PRAS40 in this way amounts to net activation of mTORC1.

edges.mechanism: 14-3-3 binds AKT-phosphorylated TSC2 at Ser939 and Thr1462, with Ser981 and the MK2-generated site Ser1210 also contributing, and partitions TSC2 into the cytosol away from the membrane compartment where it acts on Rheb; whether TSC1-TSC2 association is lost or the intact complex is displaced from the lysosomal surface remains unresolved.
edges.notes: REDD1 has been reported to displace 14-3-3 from TSC2 under hypoxia, but direct displacement remains disputed.

edges.mechanism: 14-3-3 docks onto AMPK-phosphorylated Raptor (pSer722/pSer792), suppressing mTORC1 activity toward S6K1/4E-BP1 under energy stress.
edges.notes: 14-3-3 binding was tested by mutating Ser722 and Ser792 together, and the 14-3-3-motif epitope depended mainly on Ser722.

edges.mechanism: Phosphorylated TFE3 is bound by 14-3-3 and held in the cytoplasm, mirroring the TFEB mechanism
14-3-3 binds phospho-Ser211 TFEB, masking its nuclear localisation signal and sequestering it in the cytoplasm

14-3-3 dimers bind FOXO1 after AKT phosphorylates it at Thr24 and Ser256 (binding needs both sites). Binding impairs DNA binding and shifts FOXO1 to the cytoplasm, contributing to insulin- and growth factor-induced silencing of FOXO1 target genes.
edges.notes: 14-3-3 is one of several redundant routes for FOXO1 nuclear exclusion; Ser319-cluster phosphorylation and leucine-rich export signals also act. In HEK293 cells, overexpressed FOXO1 was excluded from the nucleus after IGF-1 stimulation without 14-3-3 binding.

edges.mechanism: Phosphorylation of FOXO3a by AKT or SGK1 creates 14-3-3 binding sites; 14-3-3 binding drives nuclear exclusion and cytoplasmic retention, terminating FOXO3a-dependent transcription.
edges.notes: FOXO3 is a Ser473-selective AKT substrate.

edges.mechanism: SGK1 phosphorylation of NEDD4-2 creates 14-3-3 binding sites; 14-3-3 binding sequesters the ligase away from ENaC, preventing PY-motif ubiquitination and increasing channel surface density.
S6K1-phosphorylated Thr1135 of Rictor recruits 14-3-3 proteins to Rictor and mTORC2. Whether this binding restrains mTORC2 signalling to AKT is unresolved.
edges.notes: A Thr1135Ala Rictor mutant increased AKT Ser473 phosphorylation in two studies, whereas phospho-site mutants left mTORC2 kinase activity or AKT phosphorylation unchanged in two others.

edges.mechanism: The YY1-PGC-1alpha complex drives transcription of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes, supporting oxidative capacity
YY1 and PGC-1alpha form a transcriptional complex on mitochondrial gene promoters whose assembly depends on mTOR activity
Active ZFP36L1 degrades SASP cytokine mRNAs; its MK2-dependent inactivation permits their accumulation
edges.notes: mTOR-dependent translation is generally required for the SASP, but the MK2-ZFP36L1 mRNA-decay mechanism rests on a single primary study.

edges.mechanism: The basolateral sodium pump sustains the electrochemical gradient that drives transepithelial reabsorption.
Unphosphorylated BAD neutralises BCL-XL and promotes apoptosis; its AKT-dependent sequestration is one arm of mTORC2-supported survival signalling.
CLC-K channels provide the basolateral chloride exit required for net salt transport.
Nuclear FOXO1 drives the hepatic gluconeogenic transcriptional programme; AKT-dependent exclusion is how insulin suppresses glucose output.
Nuclear FOXO1 drives gluconeogenic gene expression; it is inactivated by AKT once mTORC2 has phosphorylated AKT at Ser473.
Glucokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, committing hepatic glucose to glycolytic flux.
AKT phosphorylates MDM2 and promotes its nuclear translocation, where it drives p53 ubiquitination and degradation, removing p53-dependent apoptotic and cell-cycle-arrest output.
edges.notes: Whether this substrate depends on AKT hydrophobic-motif phosphorylation has not been tested.

edges.mechanism: ChREBP activates glucose-responsive lipogenic transcription in adipocytes.

The WW domains of Nedd4-2 bind PY motifs in the cytoplasmic C-termini of the ENaC subunits, and the ligase conjugates ubiquitin to lysines in their N-terminal tails, driving channel retrieval and degradation and lowering apical sodium conductance.
sites: N-terminal cytoplasmic lysines of the ENaC subunits

edges.mechanism: Rac1·GTP drives branched actin polymerisation in dendritic spines.
Rac1-driven actin polymerisation is the structural arm of L-LTP, distinct from the mTORC1-dependent translational arm.
Spine density falls with loss of the mTORC2-Tiam1-Rac1 actin-polymerisation arm.
ENaC provides the rate-limiting apical entry step for sodium reabsorption in the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron.
GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane is the proximate step in insulin-stimulated glucose uptake.
AS160 GAP activity keeps its Rab substrates GDP-loaded and retains GLUT4 vesicles intracellularly until AKT phosphorylation relieves it.
edges.notes: GAP polarity: negative regulator of GLUT4 translocation. External reference not independently verified.

edges.mechanism: Tiam1 is a Rac1-specific GEF, loading Rac1 with GTP; GEF polarity is positive.
Tiam1 is the Rac1 guanine-nucleotide exchange factor through which mTORC2 drives actin polymerisation in the consolidation of long-term memory.

Rhythmically phosphorylated BMAL1 associates with the cap-binding machinery and promotes cap-dependent translation, which would confer a circadian rhythm on bulk protein synthesis independently of its transcriptional output.
edges.notes: Reported by one laboratory and not yet independently replicated; rhythmic mTORC1 activity could by itself account for the rhythm in protein synthesis.

edges.mechanism: BMAL1 is the obligate bHLH-PAS partner of CLOCK; the heterodimer is the DNA-binding unit that drives E-box transcription.
S6K1-phosphorylated BMAL1 associates with the cap-binding translation machinery, acting as a rhythmic accessory factor at eIF4F rather than only as a transcription factor.
edges.context: mouse liver, cap-binding and polysome fractions
edges.notes: Reported in Lipton 2015; whether the contact with eIF4E is direct, and its stoichiometry, are not settled.

edges.mechanism: BMAL1 acts as a negative regulator of mTORC1; Bmal1-null tissues show elevated mTORC1 activity, placing the clock's positive limb upstream of the kinase.
edges.notes: The intermediates between BMAL1 and mTORC1 are not fully defined.

edges.mechanism: CLOCK heterodimerises with BMAL1 through their PAS domains to form the positive-limb transcription factor of the mammalian oscillator.
CLOCK–BMAL1 drives E-box-dependent transcription of Cry1, which then returns to repress the heterodimer — the core delayed negative feedback loop.
Ddit4 (REDD1), a TSC-dependent inhibitor of mTORC1, is rhythmically expressed in mouse peripheral tissues, offering a candidate transcriptional route from the clock to mTORC1 restraint.
edges.context: mouse peripheral tissues, circadian transcriptome atlas
edges.notes: Rhythmic Ddit4 expression is documented in circadian transcriptome datasets (PMID 25349387: Zhang R et al., PNAS 2014;111(45):16219-16224), but that reference supports rhythmicity only: direct CLOCK-BMAL1 occupancy at the locus is not established and the glucocorticoid rhythm is an alternative driver, hence the emerging grading. Sestrin rhythmicity is not well documented.

edges.mechanism: CLOCK–BMAL1 drives rhythmic transcription of Nr1d1 (Rev-erbα) through E-boxes, initiating the accessory stabilising loop
CLOCK–BMAL1 heterodimer binds E-boxes in the Per1 promoter and drives its rhythmic transcription
CLOCK–BMAL1 binds E-boxes in the Per2 promoter to drive its rhythmic transcription, generating the PER2 oscillation that times TSC1 recruitment to mTORC1.
CRY1 binds the CLOCK–BMAL1 heterodimer on DNA and blocks its transactivation, closing the negative limb of the feedback loop.
CRY1 is the repressive subunit of the PER–CRY complex; PER proteins control its nuclear entry and stability
CK1ε phosphorylation creates the phosphodegron that targets PER2 for ubiquitin-dependent degradation, shortening PER2 half-life and advancing clock phase
REV-ERBα represses Bmal1 transcription through RORE elements, generating the antiphase BMAL1 rhythm that sets the timing of BMAL1-dependent mTORC1 restraint
The nuclear PER–CRY complex binds CLOCK–BMAL1 and represses its transactivation, closing the core negative feedback loop
edges.notes: External identifier requires independent verification.

edges.mechanism: VIP-mediated coupling between SCN neurons is required for network synchrony and for normal entrainment of behavioural rhythms to light
edges.notes: The Aton 2005 PMID is given from memory and should be verified.

edges.mechanism: VIP signalling through VPAC2 receptors is required for synchrony and sustained rhythmicity among SCN neurons; it is the route by which 4E-BP1-dependent translation reaches network behaviour.
edges.notes: PMID 15750589 (Aton SJ et al., Nat Neurosci 2005;8(4):476-483).

edges.mechanism: Progressive accumulation and aggregation of amyloid-beta is a defining neuropathological feature of Alzheimer's disease and is causally sufficient in the autosomal dominant forms caused by APP and presenilin mutations, although its primacy in sporadic disease remains debated; this aggregate burden is also the target of the autophagy-based rationale for mTOR inhibition.
edges.notes: In transgenic Alzheimer models, mTOR inhibition lowers brain amyloid-beta and improves cognition when started before substantial pathology has accumulated, and the benefit depends on intact autophagy; no controlled human efficacy data exist.

edges.mechanism: Polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin aggregation drives Huntington's disease pathology.

Alpha-synuclein is the aggregating protein of the synucleinopathies and is cleared by macroautophagy and the proteasome, which is the route that mTOR inhibition is intended to engage in Parkinson disease models.
mTORC1-dependent translation is selective (structured-5'UTR and TOP mRNAs) rather than global, so mTORC1 inhibition only partly reduces bulk protein synthesis.
mTORC1-driven translation of IL1A and MAPKAPK2 mRNAs is required for the senescence-associated secretory phenotype; rapamycin suppresses SASP without clearing senescent cells.
Net protein accumulation from enhanced initiation, elongation and ribosome supply drives increase in cell mass.
Coordinated rRNA transcription/processing, ribosomal-protein translation and nucleolar assembly produce mature 40S/60S subunits.
Autophagic lysosome reformation regenerates the lysosomal pool consumed during autophagy, closing the amino-acid/mTORC1 oscillatory loop.
Completed autophagolysosomal degradation replenishes the lysosomal and cytosolic amino-acid pools
Completed autophagolysosomal degradation of cytoplasmic protein replenishes free amino acid pools
Amino acids liberated by autophagic degradation reactivate mTORC1, making the system oscillatory rather than switch-like, a feature with implications for drug kinetics.
Pharmacological mTOR inhibition induces autophagy and accelerates clearance of amyloid-beta in cellular and animal models.
Polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin is cleared by macroautophagy; rapamycin or CCI-779 reduces aggregates and improves outcomes in model organisms.
Suppressed autophagy is one of the two named mechanisms (with ER stress) through which chronic mTORC1 activation produces beta-cell dedifferentiation and failure.
Neural-specific deletion of Atg5 or Atg7 alone, with no disease mutant present, causes progressive motor deficits, ubiquitin-positive inclusions and neurodegeneration.
edges.notes: Neurons cannot dilute damaged proteins by division, so basal flux carries more weight than in renewing tissue.

edges.mechanism: Alpha-synuclein is degraded by both macroautophagy and the proteasome, and mTOR inhibition with rapamycin lowers its levels in cells and is neuroprotective in cellular and animal models of Parkinson's disease; the fly and mouse aggregate-clearance data obtained with rapamycin and CCI-779 come from polyglutamine models and do not themselves demonstrate clearance of alpha-synuclein in vivo.
CLEAR target genes include core autophagy genes, so TFEB activation raises autophagic flux as well as lysosomal capacity
Coordinate induction of lysosomal hydrolases, membrane proteins and v-ATPase subunits expands lysosomal number and degradative capacity
The oxidative arm of the pentose phosphate pathway, activated by SREBP-driven G6PD expression downstream of mTORC1, generates NADPH.
edges.notes: The oxidative pentose phosphate pathway supplies NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate.

edges.mechanism: The pentose phosphate pathway generates ribose-5-phosphate, the pentose backbone for nucleotide synthesis.
Actin polymerisation, not translational control, is the mTORC2-dependent requirement for late-phase LTP.
SGK1-driven distal nephron sodium reabsorption sustains extracellular volume and blood pressure; its failure produces salt wasting and hypotension.
Rictor deletion impairs long-term memory alongside L-LTP while sparing short-term memory.
Autophagic and lysosomal flux are under circadian control, so the magnitude of any mTORC1-dependent autophagy readout depends on sampling time — a confounder rarely addressed.
edges.notes: Rhythmic autophagic and lysosomal flux is documented in the primary literature: PMID 21897364 (Ma D, Panda S, Lin JD, 'Temporal orchestration of circadian autophagy rhythm by C/EBPbeta', EMBO J 2011;30(22):4642-4651).

edges.mechanism: The clock imposes a daily rhythm on translation initiation and ribosome biogenesis, including rhythmic TOP mRNA translation driven by rhythmic mTORC1–S6K1 activity and by S6K1-phosphorylated BMAL1
edges.notes: PMID corrected from 23300385 (an unrelated PLoS Biol neuroimaging paper) to 23300384, verified against PubMed as Jouffe C et al., 'The circadian clock coordinates ribosome biogenesis', PLoS Biol 2013;11(1):e1001455.

edges.mechanism: Rhythmic expression of C/EBPβ is one clock output that times the hepatic autophagy gene programme

mTORC1 activity is itself rhythmic: PER2-dependent restraint operates in a time-of-day-dependent manner and the response of hepatic mTOR signalling to caloric restriction varies with time of day, so any mTORC1-dependent readout depends on sampling time
edges.notes: Methodological consequence: the time of day at which samples are taken affects measured mTORC1 activity.

edges.mechanism: S6K1 phosphorylation and downstream ribosome biogenesis oscillate over the day in liver, so mTORC1 output is itself a rhythmic variable rather than a constant baseline.
edges.context: mouse liver, polysome and ribosome profiling
edges.notes: PMID corrected from 23620741 (an unrelated PLoS One HIV capsid paper) to 23300384, verified against PubMed as Jouffe C et al., 'The circadian clock coordinates ribosome biogenesis', PLoS Biol 2013;11(1):e1001455.

edges.mechanism: Feeding- and clock-driven rhythms in mTORC1 activity impose a daily rhythm on TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation, coupling the lysosomal–autophagic programme to time of day
edges.notes: PMID corrected from 30988016 (which is Maslon MM, EMBO J 2019;38(9), a different paper in the same journal and year) to 31126958, verified against PubMed as Pastore N et al., 'Nutrient-sensitive transcription factors TFEB and TFE3 couple autophagy and metabolism to the peripheral clock', EMBO J 2019;38(12):e101347.

edges.mechanism: The GATOR1-related familial focal epilepsies account for a substantial proportion of familial focal epilepsy and carry elevated risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy.
Hyperactivity reported alongside sleep–wake disturbance and hyperphagia as a recognised feature of the extended Smith–Kingsmore phenotype

Hyperphagia emerged as a recognised feature in a cohort of 28 individuals carrying nine pathogenic MTOR variants; it is mechanistically expected from hypothalamic mTORC1 nutrient sensing rather than incidental.
In a cohort of 28 individuals carrying nine pathogenic MTOR variants, sleep–wake disturbance emerged as a recognised feature alongside hyperphagia and hyperactivity.
edges.notes: Recognised in a single cohort of 28 individuals carrying nine pathogenic MTOR variants, alongside hyperphagia and hyperactivity.

edges.mechanism: Hyperphagia and hyperactivity are recognised features in a cohort of 28 individuals with nine pathogenic MTOR variants, as hypothalamic nutrient sensing predicts.
edges.notes: Sleep-wake disturbance, hyperphagia and hyperactivity are the recognised features of this cohort; obesity as such is not reported, and hyperphagic obesity is the phenotype of POMC-neuron Tsc1 deletion in mice. Central hyperphagia is mechanistically expected from arcuate nucleus mTORC1 nutrient sensing rather than incidental.

edges.mechanism: Focal cortical dysplasia type II presents with drug-resistant focal epilepsy; management is surgical, with mTOR inhibition investigational.
Hemimegalencephaly presents with hemispheric enlargement and severe epilepsy.
Epilepsy is a core feature of tuberous sclerosis complex alongside cortical tubers, SEGA, angiomyolipoma and LAM; refractory focal seizures are an approved everolimus indication.

Anabolic resistance is defined as a blunted muscle protein-synthesis response to amino acids and to loading; mechanism is multifactorial (reduced sensitivity of the mTORC1 machinery, impaired postprandial perfusion and amino-acid delivery, splanchnic extraction).
The SASP is the secretory programme of senescent cells; the distinction matters because rapamycin suppresses the secretome without removing the cells.

Thymic involution, contraction of the naive repertoire, accumulation of PD-1+ exhausted-like cells and inflammaging together degrade the response to vaccination, which is why vaccine response became the testing ground for geroprotective mTOR inhibition.
